groups.title: The night bus trial
groups.stimulus: When Harlowe introduced a Friday night bus between its station and the northern estates, passengers could board without booking. The route followed the daytime service until the ring road, then skipped four stops near closed shops. The transport office expected most use just after the last train. Drivers instead recorded two distinct surges, one after the last train and one around midnight, when cleaners and kitchen workers changed shifts. A rider survey suggested the later group had previously shared taxis. The survey was handed out only on board, so it could not establish how many people still relied on taxis. A local employer asked the council to move the midnight departure twenty minutes earlier. The office kept the original time for a second month, explaining that changing both the timetable and the fare would make it harder to interpret new ridership figures. The lower fare was funded out of unused trial money. When use rose, the office did not claim that the fare alone was responsible: the service had by then also appeared on journey planners. The station announced the service over its loudspeakers only during the final week. After the trial ended, the council proposed a similar service for Saturday but said that any decision would require separate evidence about Saturday travel.

questions.stem: The trial route stopped at all the same places as the daytime service.
questions.explanation: It skipped four stops near closed shops.

questions.stem: The largest group of survey respondents had previously travelled by taxi.
questions.explanation: The passage mentions taxi sharing among the later group but supplies no overall survey ranking.

questions.stem: The lower fare was paid for with money left over from the trial budget.
questions.explanation: It was funded by unused trial money.

questions.stem: The office kept the midnight departure unchanged partly to make later ridership data easier to interpret.
questions.explanation: Holding time fixed while the fare changed made subsequent ridership figures easier to interpret.

groups.title: The boatyard bell
groups.stimulus: A brass bell hangs in North Quay's museum. Its label once said it had summoned boatyard workers since 1860. The date came from an entry in the yard ledger: 'bell and fittings, twelve shillings'. A conservator noticed that the surviving bell's bracket would have required bolts of a size that the yard did not order until decades later. That did not settle the date of the bell itself: a reused bell might have been given a new bracket. No maker's mark was visible. A volunteer then found two photographs. The earlier one showed a bell of roughly the right proportions on a wooden frame, but its rim was hidden. The later one clearly showed the present bell on the warehouse wall. In the years between the two pictures, the yard lost its records in a flood. The museum removed the ledger date from the object label and put it on an adjacent panel explaining the evidence. A former employee complained that visitors wanted a date, not a list of doubts. The conservator replied that the later photograph provided just such a date, but it was a date by which the bell was present, not necessarily the year it arrived. The museum kept a recording of the former employee's account alongside the panel.

questions.stem: What is the main significance of the later photograph?
options: It dates the flood that destroyed the earlier records.
It proves the surviving bracket was fitted in 1860.
It identifies the maker of the bell.
It gives a latest possible bound for the bell's arrival at the yard.
questions.explanation: The bell was demonstrably already present in that photograph.

questions.stem: Why did the conservator not use the bolt sizes to date the bell itself?
options: The relevant order entries were all lost in the flood.
The bell could have been attached to a bracket fitted later.
The early photograph clearly showed the current bracket.
The yard always ordered bolts after completing a job.
questions.explanation: The surviving mount need not be original to the bell.

questions.stem: What prevents the earlier photograph from conclusively identifying the bell?
options: It depicts a different-sized bell from the one in the museum.
The wooden frame does not appear anywhere else.
A distinguishing part of the bell is not visible.
The photograph was made after the flood.
questions.explanation: The shape appears similar but its rim is hidden.

questions.stem: Why did the museum move the ledger date to a separate panel?
options: To show that the ledger dated from after the photographs
To replace documentary evidence with testimony
To keep the date hidden from most visitors
To present it as evidence without treating it as the object's established date
questions.explanation: The entry remains relevant but cannot securely identify the surviving bell.

groups.title: Seed library
groups.stimulus: Riverside Library's seed shelves opened with a simple invitation: take a labelled envelope and, if your plants produce seeds, return some in autumn. Volunteers initially counted envelopes taken as a sign of success. The figure doubled in the second year, but the number of varieties returned fell. Some popular beans had been distributed in larger envelopes, so fewer households could grow the same variety before supplies ran out. As an experiment, volunteers divided those stocks into smaller envelopes the following spring. Gardeners with tiny plots found the change helpful; two allotment groups said that using several envelopes for a shared bed made record keeping awkward. The seed team offered those groups a single bulk envelope on request. It also stopped treating a return of any seed as evidence that a variety was preserved. For one squash, seeds from neighbouring plants had mixed, so the new plants did not consistently resemble those described on the envelopes. A volunteer proposed replacing all squash with beans, whose labels had caused fewer problems. The team instead kept squash but explained the difficulty on its signs. It introduced a second sign asking growers to record whether seeds came from plants they had isolated. The next annual report listed participation and the number of reliably identified varieties as separate outcomes.

questions.stem: The seed team required everyone who took an envelope to return seeds.
questions.explanation: The invitation to return seed was conditional, not a requirement.

questions.stem: Before the smaller packets were trialled, the size of some envelopes limited how many households could receive those beans.
questions.explanation: Larger packets ran down those stocks after fewer households had received them.

questions.stem: The bulk-envelope option was taken up by both allotment groups.
questions.explanation: The option was offered, but the text does not report uptake.

questions.stem: The smaller envelopes solved the record-keeping problem reported by the allotment groups.
questions.explanation: Those groups said using multiple envelopes made records harder; the alternative was a bulk envelope.

groups.title: A map of shade
groups.stimulus: At lunchtime a team mapped the shade along a proposed walking route for older residents. It used aerial photographs to estimate where trees blocked the sun. The first map picked an alley with dense branches even though the alley ran beside a wall that gave off heat in the afternoon. A volunteer walking the route noted that people could cross the street to avoid the wall but would then lose the trees' cover. The team added sensors at shoulder height along both sides and measured temperatures for a week. One day cloud reduced the contrast, and the team reported this rather than omitting it as an exception. Its preferred path ended up crossing an open square that appeared unattractive on the shade map. The square had seating under a broad canopy halfway across and drinking water near the far exit. On subsequent walks the team found that the canopy was closed occasionally for maintenance; it left those dates off a leaflet only because they changed weekly, not because closures were rare. The leaflet instead linked to a live notice. When a councillor asked for one route that could be recommended all year, the team explained that a path pleasant at summer lunchtime might offer little protection from winter wind.

questions.stem: What prompted measurements on both sides of the alley?
options: The trade-off between shade and heat from the wall
A request to measure winter winds
A complaint that sensors were mounted too low
A closure of the square's canopy
questions.explanation: Crossing the street avoided the warm wall but lost the tree cover, so both sides needed checking.

questions.stem: How did the team handle measurements taken on a cloudy day?
options: It used only readings from the wall side of the street.
It repeated the day in direct sunlight and reported only that result.
It incorporated the readings into a winter-only temperature estimate.
It kept and reported the reduced contrast.
questions.explanation: It reported the effect rather than discarding the day.

questions.stem: What advantage did the leaflet's live notice have over printing closure dates?
options: It showed which closures would occur every month of the year.
It meant the team could stop observing how seating affected the route.
It could communicate maintenance dates that changed from week to week.
It made the crossing sheltered even when the canopy was closed.
questions.explanation: The dates on a printed leaflet could quickly become out of date.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about the aerial photographs?
options: They showed that the square was protected from winter wind.
They were used only after the route was selected.
They supplied one useful input but overlooked other features affecting the route.
They were considered unreliable for locating trees.
questions.explanation: They estimated shade, not the wall's heat, water availability or the usefulness of seating.

groups.title: A quiet collection
groups.stimulus: The community archive announced that a collection of factory recordings would be available in its listening room. Each recording had two versions: an unedited file kept by the archive and an access copy that could omit a short section if a speaker had asked for that condition when donating it. Some speakers wanted names removed but retained references to job titles. One interviewer argued that retaining titles might still make particular workers identifiable. The archivist agreed and reopened discussions with the speakers rather than automatically applying more cuts. At the public launch, a visitor asked why every conversation did not have a written transcript. The archive had enough funding to transcribe interviews on request but not to transcribe the entire collection in advance. After six months, popular recordings had attracted several requests each, while some had attracted none. Staff started offering short summaries to help users choose, taking care not to disclose details omitted from the access copies. Enquiries about the less familiar recordings rose at the next open day. Staff were reluctant to attribute the rise solely to the summaries, as the open day included an exhibition about a department previously overlooked by researchers. The listening room remained open throughout the period, though some recordings were not available to borrow or download.

questions.stem: Why did the archivist reopen discussions with speakers?
options: Removing names might not by itself prevent identification.
The interviewer claimed job titles had no value.
Speakers had asked for all transcripts to be withdrawn.
The unedited copies had been deleted.
questions.explanation: Retained job titles could still identify particular workers.

questions.stem: What did availability in the listening room imply about borrowing or downloading?
options: Only recordings with transcripts could be borrowed.
The unedited files could always be downloaded.
The restrictions applied only during the launch.
A recording might be available to listen to without being available to take away.
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes room access from borrowing or download.

questions.stem: Why was the increase in open-day enquiries hard to attribute to the summaries?
options: Less familiar recordings were moved to a different archive.
Regular users were prohibited from requesting transcripts.
Summaries omitted all references to the department in the exhibition.
The exhibition also drew attention to a previously overlooked department.
questions.explanation: Both offered potential explanations for growing interest.

questions.stem: What problem were the short summaries designed to solve?
options: Avoiding discussion with speakers about conditions
Guaranteeing equal requests for each interview
Helping users decide which recordings to request
questions.explanation: Without full transcripts in advance, users needed another way to explore what was available.

groups.title: The useful puddle
groups.stimulus: A housing association proposed levelling a courtyard because residents complained about a large puddle near the bins. Before work began, an engineer discovered that the depression directed water away from the basement of the neighbouring building. Filling it alone would risk moving the problem rather than solving it. A second proposal added a drain to the street. The water company warned that the street pipe already ran close to capacity after heavy rain, even though it could accept more water in ordinary weather. A gardener suggested a planted basin on the same spot, with a raised route to the bins. Most rain would soak into the soil there, but a shallow channel would direct excess flow to the original safe area of the courtyard. The association tested the design with a model and then built a pilot. It measured how long standing water remained after a storm, not just how often water collected. One year later, residents reported dry access to the bins more often, although the planted basin itself still filled in wet weather. Some visitors assumed the basin had failed when they saw the water. A notice explained that temporary storage was intentional. The association said that a later review would assess maintenance costs separately from the improvement in access.

questions.stem: Why might a visitor misjudge the basin's performance after a storm?
options: A normal storage function looked like continuing waterlogging.
The basin was meant to replace the route to the bins.
The raised path was intended to overflow into the street drain.
Water disappeared before the plants had time to soak it up.
questions.explanation: Some visitors interpreted water in the basin as failure, although it was meant to fill temporarily.

questions.stem: What risk did the engineer identify in filling the original depression alone?
options: Water might be diverted towards the nearby basement.
The bins would require more regular collection.
The raised route would become too steep.
The planted basin would need replacing.
questions.explanation: The depression was protecting the basement by directing water away.

questions.stem: What question did the association leave for a later review?
options: Whether the street could receive ordinary-weather drainage.
Whether the surveyed depression was protecting the basement.
What the design would cost to maintain.
Whether dry access had ever improved.
questions.explanation: The improvement in access was already reported, but maintenance costs were still to be assessed.

questions.stem: Which measure best captures the residents' practical benefit in the account?
options: The material chosen for the raised route
Lower pressure in the street pipe in ordinary weather
More frequent dry access to the bins
questions.explanation: Residents explicitly reported this improvement even when the basin held water.

groups.title: The bakery clock
groups.stimulus: A bakery promised that customers who ordered online by noon could collect bread from four o'clock. After three weeks, it found that orders completed just before noon were more likely to be late than orders completed in the morning. The manager first assumed late orders tended to be larger. Records showed no difference in typical order size, but the late orders included more loaves that needed a long proving time. Moving the deadline to eleven for all orders would have made planning simpler. The manager instead moved only the deadline for those loaves. The ordering site initially displayed the change in small print, and several customers assumed the earlier deadline applied to everything. Staff revised the page so that each product showed its own cut-off. On-time collections improved the following month. The manager cautioned that the web change coincided with using a second oven on Fridays. To identify how much each change contributed, staff compared Fridays with other days. Friday collections improved more than collections on other days, but Fridays also had the worst starting performance. As an additional check the bakery decided to track performance on days when the spare oven was out of use. It did not change the promise about collection from four during the trial.

questions.stem: Which discovery justified changing the deadline for only some loaves?
options: All online orders near noon missed the collection promise.
Orders near noon included more loaves requiring a longer proving time.
Morning orders were usually larger but involved fewer product lines.
Small orders near noon usually came from customers collecting on Friday.
questions.explanation: The key difference was the mix of products, not typical order size.

questions.stem: Which new observation would be most useful for examining performance without help from the second oven?
options: The number of times staff explained the cut-off in person
Performance after the web revision on days the spare oven is not used
The typical price of online orders before the trial
Customer estimates of the oven's age
questions.explanation: This can show whether improvement occurs without the oven change.

questions.stem: Why did the manager not treat the first month's improvement as proof that the revised page alone worked?
options: All deadlines were moved back by one hour.
Staff had moved the collection time on every day.
The second oven was introduced at the same time on Fridays.
questions.explanation: A simultaneous change could account for some of the improvement.

questions.stem: What was the weakness in comparing Friday to the other days after the changes?
options: Typical order sizes had increased only on Friday.
No Friday collections had been measured before the changes.
Friday began with worse performance and had more room to improve.
Only Friday had adopted the product-specific cut-offs.
questions.explanation: Friday's lower starting performance complicates an attribution to the spare oven.

groups.title: Tracing a tune
groups.stimulus: On a collection of harbour songs, one tune appears in versions recorded at towns more than a hundred miles apart. An editor originally called the southern version an imitation of the northern one because hers was the oldest surviving recording. A musician pointed out that the dates of recordings indicate when someone happened to collect a tune, not when it was composed. The northern recording was made by an enthusiast who never travelled south. In the southern town a dance programme printed before either recording listed a tune with the same name. That programme recorded a title but no music, and a different tune might have used the same title. The editor changed the booklet to describe the relationship as uncertain. An amateur researcher subsequently found a notebook with melodies copied in pencil, including one close to the southern version. The notebook carried a date on its cover, but later pages contained references to an event held much later. The archive digitised the notebook with page order preserved so readers could see these clues for themselves. It did not announce that the tune originated in the south. The new edition used the two recordings to illustrate how strongly a single tune can change when adapted to different dance patterns, regardless of its point of origin.

questions.stem: What distinction undermined the editor's first claim?
options: The date a tune was documented is not necessarily the date it began.
A title is more reliable than a recording.
Dance tunes do not travel between towns.
An older recording must be an imitation.
questions.explanation: An earlier recording establishes documentation, not musical origin.

questions.stem: Why did the dance programme not prove that the southern melody existed by its printing date?
options: The southern recording used a different title from the programme.
The programme showed a later date than the southern recording.
It listed a title that could have been used for a different tune.
The listed tunes were demonstrably copied from the northern recording.
questions.explanation: The programme did not include the notes needed to match the tune.

questions.stem: What did events mentioned on later pages show about the notebook?
options: The relevant tune page was recorded in the south.
The cover date was not a reliable date for all the entries.
The cover had been added after the notebook was scanned.
All entries were written after both recordings.
questions.explanation: Later references show not everything could have been written at the time given by the cover.

questions.stem: What purpose do the recordings serve in the new edition?
options: They illustrate variation across dance uses without settling origin.
They show both towns used identical dance patterns.
They prove that the southern dance programme used the northern melody.
They confirm the date printed on the notebook cover.
questions.explanation: The edition emphasises adaptation rather than assigning a birthplace.

groups.title: Lift weights
groups.stimulus: A small furniture workshop replaced a rule requiring two people for every load above a stated weight. Its manager had noticed workers moving light but awkward panels alone, even though those panels could block their view. The new system recorded not only mass but shape, handholds and the distance to be travelled. Staff sorted jobs into ones that could be done alone, ones requiring a second person, and ones requiring a wheeled support regardless of crew size. In the first month the number of reported near misses rose. The manager did not regard this as straightforward evidence of worsening safety, because the reporting form had been simplified in the same week. Reports also began to describe risks that were not covered by the original weight rule. A few older employees worried that using a trolley would slow them down. When the workshop timed completed jobs rather than individual lifts, some jobs took less time with a trolley because fewer pieces had to be carried separately. That result did not apply to the narrow room where the trolley could not turn, and the manager kept a different procedure there. The company planned to review the effect after a full quarter, when it would have records from the busier season as well.

questions.stem: A trolley reduced the time taken for at least some jobs by reducing the number of separate carries.
questions.explanation: The timing exercise found that some complete jobs were faster because fewer pieces had to be carried separately.

questions.stem: Reported near misses fell in the first month.
questions.explanation: They rose, although the rise did not necessarily indicate more danger.

questions.stem: The number of injuries in the busy season exceeded the previous year's.
questions.explanation: No busy-season injury totals or comparison are provided.

questions.stem: The narrow room retained a different procedure because the trolley could not turn there.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly gives that reason for the exception.

groups.title: The borrowed telescope
groups.stimulus: A town science centre lent small telescopes for a month at a time. At first, households had to collect equipment in person on a Saturday afternoon, because volunteers wanted to demonstrate how to align a finder. Demand filled all slots while a waiting list grew. A youth club suggested that the centre loan telescopes through several branch libraries. Staff liked the idea but knew branch employees could not provide an extended demonstration. They trialled a short video that borrowers could view before collection and included a card pointing to an optional evening help session. Central staff then recorded that the proportion of borrowers attending help in person was lower than before. They did not know how many watched the video unless they watched it on the centre's own website; the branches were free to show it on a shared screen. The next borrower survey therefore asked people where they had watched any instruction. Not all borrowers replied. Loan return rates remained similar whether equipment was collected centrally or at a branch, but loan extensions were more common at branches. One volunteer noted that branch telescopes had been distributed during a particularly cloudy month. The annual report presented these observations without asserting that the new location caused borrowers to keep equipment longer.

questions.stem: Which inference is least justified?
options: Moving collection to libraries caused loan extensions to become more common.
Borrowers could still get help in person.
Some views were not captured by the centre's website data.
Return rates were roughly similar across locations.
questions.explanation: The cloudy month and other factors may explain the association.

questions.stem: How did staff preserve access to help after introducing branch collection?
options: They paired video instruction with optional in-person help in the evening.
They limited new borrowers to branches with full-time technical staff.
They required branch employees to teach alignment.
They provided the original demonstration to all branch borrowers on Saturdays.
questions.explanation: This substituted for the original extended demonstration at pickup.

questions.stem: What did the centre know about shared-screen views at branches?
options: Every shared-screen user replied to the borrower survey.
Such views could occur without showing up as individual website views.
The centre could count a view only if the borrower also visited its help session.
The screens were the main means of instruction for most branch users.
questions.explanation: Branches could show the video collectively; the centre's website could not count those viewers individually.

questions.stem: Why did the new survey ask where instructions had been watched?
options: To capture viewing that website figures alone would miss
To determine how cloudy the month was
To check whether borrowers collected on Saturdays
To decide whether to stop allowing renewals
questions.explanation: A video could be shown off-site on a shared screen without registering individual views.

groups.title: Turning waste into colour
groups.stimulus: A design cooperative trialled dyes made from onion skins collected from three markets. It described the first batch as low-waste, not because dyeing produced no waste, but because it found an additional use for material usually thrown away. The team used tap water and a mineral fixative to help the colour stay on cloth. Its first public demonstration produced a rich orange; a later production run looked paler. The technicians discovered that the skins had been weighed before drying at the demonstration and after drying in the production run, so the recorded weights could not be compared as though they described the same thing. They also noted that the two batches had been heated for different lengths of time. The team standardised both the weighing method and the heating schedule for future batches. In a customer survey, some respondents said they preferred a range of shades to perfect uniformity. The cooperative retained the more consistent method but sold shorter runs, labelling them by batch so buyers could match fabric across a project. It did not claim its product was environmentally preferable to every synthetic dye. For that comparison it would need, among other measures, data on energy, water and what happened to dye residues after use.

questions.stem: Why was the first batch described as low-waste?
options: It made use of skins that would usually be discarded.
Customers used less fabric per project.
All dye residues were recovered for reuse.
It required no water or fixative.
questions.explanation: The claim is about reuse of input material, not the total absence of waste.

questions.stem: What new measure addressed uncertainty about future shade differences?
options: Making customers approve each dye shade before it was produced.
Using the same weighing method and heating schedule in each batch.
Reducing tap-water use to the level recorded at the demonstration.
Replacing the reused skins with a single synthetic ingredient.
questions.explanation: Two potential sources of variation were standardised together.

questions.stem: Which claim did the cooperative withhold pending broader data?
options: That the second run was visibly paler than the first.
That retailers could match lengths sold with the same batch label.
That its dye was environmentally preferable to every synthetic dye.
That discarded skins could be reused in dyeing.
questions.explanation: It needed measures beyond reuse of input material to support that comparison.

questions.stem: Why were the runs labelled by batch?
options: To prove the dye was greener than synthetic alternatives
To help buyers match fabric when shades varied
To distinguish the markets by name
To show the cloth had been weighed after drying
questions.explanation: Labels allow people to select fabric from a common run.

questions.stem: Every glazed tile in a crate passed inspection. Some square tiles in the crate are glazed. No tile that passed inspection is chipped. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some square tiles passed inspection.
No glazed tiles are chipped.
Every square tile passed inspection.
Some tiles that are not square passed inspection.
If a tile is chipped, it is not glazed.
questions.explanation: 1. The square glazed tiles passed. 2. Passing excludes chips. 3. Only some square tiles are known to be glazed. 4. No non-square tile is required. 5. A chipped tile did not pass; a glazed one did.

questions.stem: Five workshops A–E run in five consecutive slots. B immediately follows D; C is third; A is before E; E is not fifth. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: The valid orders are A–E–C–D–B. D is in position 4. This is the only option that holds in all of them.

questions.stem: A box contains 11 working sensors and 5 faulty ones. Two are drawn uniformly without replacement. What is the chance both are faulty?
questions.explanation: 5/16 × 4/15 = 1/12. After a success, both the remaining successes and total fall by one.

questions.stem: Should a council require event organisers to provide free tap water at large outdoor summer events? Select the strongest argument.
options: Yes; rules for event organisers are generally a sign of good management.
Yes; accessible drinking water can reduce heat-related illness when crowds cannot readily leave a site.
No; outdoor events can take place in cool weather too.
No; some people would rather buy a drink other than water.
questions.explanation: The first argument connects the requirement to a foreseeable health risk under the stated conditions.

questions.stem: Only A: 17; only B: 19; only C: 12; A and B only: 7; A and C only: 9; B and C only: 6; all three: 4; none: 13. How many participants belong to exactly two of clubs A, B and C?
questions.explanation: The relevant non-overlapping regions are AB, AC, BC: 7 + 9 + 6 = 22.

questions.stem: A survey of 300 station users asked whether departures were easy to find. Of the 180 users of the electronic display, 144 said yes; of the 120 who did not use it, 96 said yes. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Exactly the same number said yes in the two groups.
The display increased the chance of finding a departure.
Most people who said yes did not use the display.
The proportion saying yes is the same in both groups.
questions.explanation: 144/180 and 96/120 are both 80%, despite the different counts.

questions.stem: No delayed orders qualified for a rebate. Every premium order qualified for a rebate. Some overseas orders were delayed. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: No premium order was delayed.
Every overseas order was delayed.
Some overseas orders did not qualify for a rebate.
Every order that qualified was premium.
Some overseas orders were not premium.
questions.explanation: 1. Premium orders qualified, so could not be delayed. 2. Only some were delayed. 3. The delayed overseas orders did not qualify. 4. Other qualifying orders are possible. 5. The delayed overseas orders were not premium.

questions.stem: Five runners J–N finish without ties. K finishes immediately after M; J finishes before M; N finishes second. Which statement could be true?
questions.explanation: The valid orders are J–N–L–M–K, J–N–M–K–L, L–N–J–M–K. L is in position 3. This is the only option that holds in at least one of them.

questions.stem: Nine of 14 numbered cards carry a star. Two different cards are selected uniformly. What is the probability that at least one has a star?
questions.explanation: Subtract the chance of two failures: 1 − 5/14 × 4/13 = 81/91.

questions.stem: Should a university release anonymised course completion rates by course? Select the strongest argument.
options: Yes; there would be more figures on the university's website.
No; applicants should never use statistics to guide a decision.
Yes; completion information can help applicants compare courses if definitions and small-cohort safeguards are clear.
questions.explanation: Comparable information can aid the intended decision, and the answer accounts for interpretability and privacy.

questions.stem: Only A: 18; only B: 13; only C: 11; A and B only: 6; A and C only: 8; B and C only: 7; all three: 3; none: 9. How many members of group A belong to neither B nor C?
questions.explanation: The relevant non-overlapping regions are A: 18 = 18.

questions.stem: A permit is issued only if both a fee is paid and a certificate supplied. A certificate is supplied only if an inspection is completed. A permit was not issued. Which explanation is consistent with the facts?
options: The fee was paid and the inspection was not completed.
The permit was issued although the fee was unpaid.
The absence of a permit proves the fee was unpaid.
The certificate was supplied before any inspection was completed.
questions.explanation: An incomplete inspection can prevent supplying a certificate and hence issuing a permit; a missing permit alone does not identify the failed step.

questions.stem: Whenever storage room R is open, a supervisor is on site. No supervisor is on site while the alarm is under test. Some deliveries occurred while the alarm was under test. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some deliveries occurred while R was not open.
Some deliveries occurred without a supervisor on site.
R was open whenever a supervisor was on site.
No delivery occurred when R was open.
If R is open, the alarm is not under test.
questions.explanation: 1. Alarm tests rule out a supervisor and hence an open room. 2. The alarm-test deliveries had none. 3. The first rule works in the other direction. 4. Nothing rules out other deliveries. 5. An open room requires a supervisor, which rules out alarm testing.

questions.stem: Presentations F, G, H, I and Q use slots 1–5. H is fourth. I is immediately after F; Q is before F; G is not next to Q. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: The valid orders are Q–F–I–H–G. F is in position 2. This is the only option that holds in all of them.

questions.stem: A delivery has a 3/5 chance of using supplier A and otherwise uses B. Exactly 7 of A's 20 equally likely driver slots are electric vehicles; at B the figure is 3 of 10. What is the probability this delivery uses an electric vehicle?
questions.explanation: Weight each success rate by its route: 3/5 × 7/20 + 2/5 × 3/10 = 33/100.

questions.stem: A museum's quarterly visits rose from 400 to 500. Member visits rose from 200 to 225. Which comparison is correct?
options: Member visits increased, but their share of all visits decreased.
Both the count and the share of member visits fell.
The increase in member visits accounted for half the overall increase.
Non-member visits rose by a smaller count than member visits.
questions.explanation: Member share fell from 200/400 = 50% to 225/500 = 45% despite the rise of 25 visits.

questions.stem: Total surveyed: 89. A: 29; B: 33; C: 26; A and B: 10; A and C: 9; B and C: 12; all three: 4. Pair counts include people in all three. How many respondents belong to none of the three societies?
questions.explanation: The union is 29 + 33 + 26 − 10 − 9 − 12 + 4 = 61; subtract from 89 to get 28.

questions.stem: All protected manuscripts are stored in cabinets. Some translated manuscripts are protected. No catalogue manuscripts are stored in cabinets. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some translated manuscripts are stored in cabinets.
No catalogue manuscript is protected.
Every manuscript stored in a cabinet is protected.
Some translated manuscripts are not catalogue manuscripts.
No translated manuscript is a catalogue manuscript.
questions.explanation: 1. The protected translated manuscripts are. 2. Protection would require cabinet storage. 3. Cabinet storage does not imply protection. 4. The protected translated manuscripts cannot be catalogue manuscripts. 5. Other translated manuscripts might be catalogue manuscripts.

questions.stem: Five trips A–E use slots 1–5. C is immediately after A. D is later than B. E is fourth. B is not adjacent to E. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: The valid orders are B–A–C–E–D. C is in position 3. This is the only option that holds in all of them.

questions.stem: Eight of 19 vouchers include a meal. Two are selected uniformly without replacement. What is the probability exactly one includes a meal?
questions.explanation: Either order works: 2 × 8/19 × 11/18 = 88/171.

questions.stem: Should a laboratory publish a plain-language summary with major study results? Select the strongest argument.
options: No; some specialists will still read the full paper.
Yes; a summary can improve access for readers who lack specialist training without removing the full report.
Yes; all readers prefer shorter documents.
questions.explanation: Accessibility is directly relevant and the answer does not assume the full report is being replaced.

questions.stem: Only A: 17; only B: 21; only C: 12; A and B only: 5; A and C only: 6; B and C only: 7; all three: 3; none: 14. How many people belong to A or C, inclusive of people who belong to both?
questions.explanation: The relevant non-overlapping regions are A, C, AB, AC, BC, ABC: 17 + 12 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 3 = 50.

questions.stem: Of 360 visitors, 180 arrived before noon. Of those arriving before noon, 120 visited the roof; of all who visited the roof, 150 arrived at any time. Which conclusion follows?
options: One quarter of visitors arriving before noon visited the roof.
One sixth of visitors arriving at or after noon visited the roof.
Two thirds of roof visitors arrived before noon.
Half of visitors arriving at or after noon visited the roof.
questions.explanation: There were 150 − 120 = 30 later roof visitors out of 180 later visitors: 1/6.

questions.stem: Only staff with training may work on a solo shift. Every person on the teaching team works at least one solo shift. Some new staff are on the teaching team. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some new staff have training.
All staff with training work solo shifts.
No untrained staff are on the teaching team.
Some new staff are not on the teaching team.
Some trained staff are not new.
questions.explanation: 1. New staff on the teaching team work solo and must be trained. 2. Training is necessary, not sufficient. 3. Team membership requires solo work and thus training. 4. The facts do not require any to be outside it. 5. Everyone trained could be new.

questions.stem: If a gallery uses a temporary wall, then it uses a special mounting kit. It uses a kit only if a technician is booked. This week no technician is booked. What follows?
options: Booking a technician would force a temporary wall to be used.
The gallery uses a kit without a technician this week.
The gallery does not use a temporary wall this week.
The gallery is closed this week.
questions.explanation: No technician means no kit. A temporary wall would require a kit, so no such wall can be used.

questions.stem: Crate A has 4 white and 9 red flowers. Crate B has 5 white and 7 red flowers. One flower is drawn uniformly from each crate independently. What is the chance exactly one flower is white?
questions.explanation: Either source can supply the only success: 4/13 × (1 − 5/12) + (1 − 4/13) × 5/12 = 73/156.

questions.stem: Total surveyed: 103. A: 43; B: 35; C: 41; A and B: 10; A and C: 14; B and C: 12; all three: 4. Pair counts include people in all three. How many people are in exactly two of groups A, B and C?
questions.explanation: Remove all three from each pair total: 10 + 14 + 12 − 3 × 4 = 24.

questions.stem: Every item that is both fragile and valuable requires separate packing. No separately packed item goes in a small van. Some fragile items go in a small van. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some fragile items are not valuable.
No valuable items go in a small van.
No item that is both fragile and valuable goes in a small van.
All separately packed items are fragile.
Some fragile items are not separately packed.
questions.explanation: 1. Those in the small van cannot require separate packing and thus are not both fragile and valuable. 2. A valuable non-fragile item might go. 3. Its separate packing rules this out. 4. The requirement does not exclude other reasons for separate packing. 5. Those in a small van are not separately packed.

questions.stem: Five talks P–T occupy consecutive slots. Q is second. S immediately follows R. T is earlier than P. R is not first. Which statement could be true?
questions.explanation: The valid orders are T–Q–P–R–S, T–Q–R–S–P. P is in position 3. This is the only option that holds in at least one of them.

questions.stem: An assembly trial records 12 errors in 80 units with guide X and 15 errors in 120 units with guide Y. Assume each faulty unit accounts for exactly one error. Which comparison follows?
options: Guide Y has fewer correctly assembled units.
Both guides have identical faulty-unit rates.
Guide X has a lower faulty-unit rate.
Guide Y has a lower faulty-unit rate despite a higher error count.
questions.explanation: X has 15% faulty units; Y has 12.5%.

questions.stem: Should a school move the start time 30 minutes later? Select the strongest argument.
options: Yes; later times generally look more modern.
No; any change to a familiar timetable is wrong.
No; if after-school buses cannot be retimed, some pupils could lose their only practical journey home.
questions.explanation: Access to a practical journey is a concrete consequence of the proposed schedule change.

questions.stem: Ten of 22 lockers are occupied. Two different locker numbers are chosen uniformly. What is the probability exactly one belongs to an occupied locker?
questions.explanation: Either order works: 2 × 10/22 × 12/21 = 40/77.

questions.stem: All priority requests include a reference number. A request without a signature is rejected. Some requests with a reference number are unsigned. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some requests with a reference number are rejected.
Some priority requests are rejected.
No priority request lacks a reference number.
A signed request cannot be rejected.
Every request without a reference number is non-priority.
questions.explanation: 1. The unsigned ones are rejected. 2. Referenced does not imply priority. 3. That follows directly from the first rule. 4. Other grounds for rejection are possible. 5. This is the contrapositive of the first rule.

questions.stem: A group of four must include exactly two of A, B and C. It must also include D or E, but not both. F may join only when C joins. Which group is allowed?
questions.explanation: B, C, E and F has exactly two of A/B/C and exactly one of D/E, and C permits F.

questions.stem: Should a town extend its library opening by one evening per week? Select the strongest argument.
options: No; some residents own books already.
Yes; local usage surveys show many residents working day shifts cannot attend at current times.
No; extending one evening will not make the library open every evening.
questions.explanation: The survey identifies a group excluded by the existing timetable and directly supports an evening extension.

groups.title: Community workshop
groups.stimulus: Concession tickets cost 60% of the full price. Each session costs the venue £48 to run, whatever the attendance.

questions.stem: What is Wednesday's total ticket revenue?
questions.explanation: (12 × 8) + ((15 × 8) × 3/5) gives £168.00 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: What percentage of all available seats were booked on Tuesday and Thursday combined? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: ((((19 + 5) + 17) + 9) ÷ (32 + 36)) × 100 gives 73.5% to the stated precision.

questions.stem: Full-price bookings for Thursday rise by 3 and concessions fall by 2. What is the surplus after the venue cost?
What is the mean revenue per booking on Monday, to the nearest penny?
questions.explanation: ((14 × 7.5) + ((8 × 7.5) × 3/5)) ÷ (14 + 8) gives £6.41 to the stated precision.

groups.title: Bicycle counters
groups.stimulus: Counters record separate inbound and outbound journeys during four equal observation windows. Some people may use a counter more than once.

questions.stem: What percentage of recorded journeys in the first two windows were inbound? Give one decimal place.
What is the net outbound count (outbound minus inbound) in the last two windows combined?
All 08–10 counts were understated. Each true count is 25% larger. What is the corrected mean combined count per hour over all observed windows, to one decimal place?

The target for 16–18 is to bring outbound journeys down to no more than 55% of that window's total, without changing inbound journeys. What is the smallest whole number of outbound journeys to remove?
questions.explanation: 297 − (round down to a whole number of ((194 × 55) ÷ 45)) gives 60 journeys.

groups.title: Travelling exhibition
groups.stimulus: Crates go by van. A trip can carry both types, subject to separate limits: at most 12 large and 18 small. Each trip costs the base fee plus a charge for the distance listed, with no return charge.

questions.stem: What is the minimum transport cost to Bramley?
questions.explanation: (37 + (62 × 0.8)) × (the greater of (round up to a whole number of (14 ÷ 12)) and (round up to a whole number of (34 ÷ 18))) gives £173.20 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: What is the minimum cost difference between Fenton and Dunford, taking the smaller cost from the larger?
questions.explanation: ((35 + (40 × 0.9)) × (the greater of (round up to a whole number of (25 ÷ 12)) and (round up to a whole number of (18 ÷ 18)))) − ((32 + (49 × 1.1)) × (the greater of (round up to a whole number of (23 ÷ 12)) and (round up to a whole number of (10 ÷ 18)))) gives £41.20 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: If Elmstead's small-crate count drops by 50%, rounding up to a whole crate, how much does this save?
questions.explanation: (41 + (71 × 0.6)) × ((the greater of (round up to a whole number of (8 ÷ 12)) and (round up to a whole number of (35 ÷ 18))) − (the greater of (round up to a whole number of (8 ÷ 12)) and (round up to a whole number of ((round up to a whole number of (35 ÷ 2)) ÷ 18)))) gives £83.60 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: Bramley combines its delivery with another 8 small crates. What is the least total distance needed for the combined delivery?
questions.explanation: 62 × (the greater of (round up to a whole number of (14 ÷ 12)) and (round up to a whole number of ((34 + 8) ÷ 18))) gives 186 km.

groups.title: Water audit
groups.stimulus: A tank has a usable capacity of 5,000 L. Readings are taken at the start of each day; assume the only added water between readings is the metered refill.

questions.stem: How much water was used during Tuesday?
What was the mean daily water use from Monday through Thursday?
Friday needs the same amount of water as Monday and Thursday combined. How much must be added before Friday's use to finish Friday at 50% capacity?
By what percentage did the volume at the start of the day fall from Wednesday to Friday? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: ((3790 − 2980) ÷ 3790) × 100 gives 21.4% to the stated precision.

groups.title: Courier tariffs
groups.stimulus: For each parcel, the charge is the base price plus the stated rate for every kg above the included weight. Weights are charged exactly (not rounded up). Economy costs are shown before any surcharges.

questions.stem: For a 7.5 kg parcel on Parcelgo, what is the charge?
questions.explanation: 7.8 + ((7.5 − 4) × 0.9) gives £10.95 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: At what weight above 2 kg do Swift and Relay cost the same?
Three separate 3.5 kg parcels go by Swift. How much more is charged than if the same parcels went as one combined parcel?
Local adds a 12% surcharge to the full bill. What is the charge for a 2.25 kg parcel, to the nearest penny?
questions.explanation: (4.9 + ((2.25 − 0.5) × 2.4)) × 1.12 gives £10.19 to the stated precision.

groups.title: Skills survey
groups.stimulus: Each respondent chose one course. Counts are respondents, not hours.

questions.stem: What percentage of respondents aged 45+ chose D or B? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: ((63 + 42) ÷ (((30 + 42) + 45) + 63)) × 100 gives 58.3% to the stated precision.

questions.stem: What is the ratio of under-25 respondents taking B to all respondents taking B, as a percentage to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: (72 ÷ ((72 + 56) + 42)) × 100 gives 42.4% to the stated precision.

questions.stem: Another 20 people join C, all aged 25–44. What fraction of people taking C are then aged 25–44, expressed to one decimal place as a percentage?
questions.explanation: ((90 + 20) ÷ (((35 + 90) + 45) + 20)) × 100 gives 57.9% to the stated precision.

questions.stem: If 1 in 4 of all under-25 respondents withdraw, how many respondents remain in the whole survey?

groups.title: Solar output
groups.stimulus: Output is measured in kWh per installed panel. Savings are earned on the total output; ignore installation costs unless stated.

questions.stem: What is combined summer output for Hill and Marsh, in MWh to two decimal places (1 MWh = 1,000 kWh)?
questions.explanation: ((34 × 262) + (29 × 235)) ÷ 1000 gives 15.72 MWh to the stated precision.

questions.stem: Find the mean spring output per installed panel across Vale and Park, to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: ((48 × 158) + (52 × 145)) ÷ (48 + 52) gives 151.2 kWh to the stated precision.

questions.stem: At £0.24 per kWh, what summer-to-autumn reduction in savings does Marsh see?
questions.explanation: ((235 − 122) × 29) × 0.24 gives £786.48 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: Compared with its spring total, by what percentage is Park's summer total higher? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: ((199 − 145) ÷ 145) × 100 gives 37.2% to the stated precision.

groups.title: Festival staffing
groups.stimulus: Workers are paid for shift length minus the unpaid break. Pay is per worker; there is no overtime premium.

questions.stem: What is Stage's total wage bill?
questions.explanation: (((450 − 45) ÷ 60) × 4) × 13.6 gives £367.20 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: What are the total paid worker-hours for Gate and Help desk?
The Food break is increased by 5 minutes and all paid hours now earn 5% more. What is the new Food wage bill?
How much greater is the total original wage bill for Gate than for Help desk?

groups.title: Library equipment
groups.stimulus: There is no VAT. Each refurb kit serves one unit. The delivery fee is charged once per entire order.

questions.stem: How much is saved by buying all Readers used with kits rather than new, with equal delivery fees?
With £950 and free delivery, what will be left after buying all Scanners used with kits?
Half the Tablets are bought new and the rest used with kits. With £36 delivery, what is the total?
A used Recorder falls in price by 20%, but its kit price stays fixed. What is the percentage reduction in the combined price, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: ((63 × 1/5) ÷ (63 + 14)) × 100 gives 16.4% to the stated precision.

groups.title: Observation at the bedside
groups.stimulus: During a ward round, medical student Ada is invited to observe a wound examination. The doctor introduces Ada as part of the team without saying that she is a student. The patient draws the blanket up and asks who will be present.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Step outside promptly without explaining her role or checking the patient's preference.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: It protects privacy immediately, but clarification could support a meaningful choice if the patient wants it.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Assume that agreeing to the examination also means agreeing to be observed by a student.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Consent to clinical care does not imply consent to student observation.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether an alternative teaching encounter can be arranged later.
questions.explanation: This affects Ada's learning plan, but scarcely affects the present consent decision.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the patient can decline Ada's presence without affecting their care.
questions.explanation: A free choice is central to valid consent.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Clarify her student role and ask whether the patient is comfortable with her staying before the examination begins.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The patient needs a genuine informed choice about student presence.

groups.title: The unsigned result
groups.stimulus: Student Baqir is helping a nurse organise electronic messages. He notices a markedly abnormal result in a folder marked reviewed, but it has no named reviewer and the responsible clinician is about to leave. Baqir has not been asked to interpret any results independently.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Ask the nurse whether the missing reviewer field is usual, without specifically mentioning the abnormal result.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: A process query is useful but does not draw attention to the possible immediate risk.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate immediate action.
options: Check nearby records briefly for the reviewer before seeking help.
Mark the result personally verified without checking.
Ask the covering clinician to review the result now.
questions.explanation: Getting a qualified reviewer now addresses risk; changing the record conceals uncertainty.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Raise the result and the missing review record immediately with the responsible clinician or covering team.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: An unresolved potentially urgent finding should be handed to someone who can act.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether responsibility for following up the result has been explicitly accepted.
questions.explanation: Closed-loop handover helps prevent an important result being missed.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Phone the patient with a diagnosis based on the result alone.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This exceeds his role and risks alarming or misleading the patient.

groups.title: A personal device
groups.stimulus: Medical student Cara takes a photo of a teaching board before noticing that one corner includes a patient's full name and clinic number. The photo has synchronised to her personal cloud account. No one has yet asked about it.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Promptly disclose the incident through the placement process and follow advice on containing local and synced copies.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The team can assess the breach and coordinate containment.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Share a cropped version in a student chat before checking whether any identifiers remain.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Unverified cropping can disclose information again through an unauthorised channel.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the photo may be recoverable outside the visible camera roll.
questions.explanation: Synced and backup copies affect containment.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the photo was taken only to review the teaching and with no intention of sharing it.
questions.explanation: Intent may inform follow-up, but does not remove the risk or the need to report.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Disable further syncing immediately but delay notifying the placement until the end of the week.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Stopping sync helps contain it, but the existing copy and delay still matter.

groups.title: A costly shortcut
groups.stimulus: On a placement, a clinician asks student Dan to enter a routine examination as completed before they have seen the patient, saying the result will be updated later. Dan knows the next team can already see the record.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Enter the record exactly as requested and plan to correct it next shift.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: False documentation can affect care before anyone corrects it.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate response to the request.
options: Decline for now without clarifying the reason.
State that it is not done yet and offer to record it after it happens.
questions.explanation: Accurate status plus direct explanation is best; misleading paperwork is worst.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Decline to record an examination that has not happened and explain the risk to the next team.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Notes must accurately reflect what happened when others will rely on them.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether another team could rely on the premature entry.
questions.explanation: The entry could cause downstream decisions to be made on false information.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Tell the clinician he will leave the examination field blank but not say why.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This avoids a false entry; explaining the issue would better prevent recurrence or misunderstanding.

groups.title: The missed handover
groups.stimulus: Student Eleni has promised to tell the evening team that a patient has been waiting for help to reach the toilet. She sees the patient's call light still on. The first nurse she approaches says she is about to start a break.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the allocated nurse is about to start a break.
questions.explanation: Availability affects whom to contact now. It does not reduce the urgency of obtaining help.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the patient is likely to attempt to walk unaided while waiting.
questions.explanation: A foreseeable fall risk changes the urgency.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Alert the covering staff now and check that someone has accepted responsibility for helping.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The patient may try to mobilise alone; a named handover helps address the immediate need.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Turn off the light so the patient will not keep attracting attention.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: That removes access to assistance without meeting the need.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Add the task to a written handover sheet but do not tell anyone directly.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: A note helps continuity but may not be seen in time.

groups.title: Identifying a person
groups.stimulus: Student Faisal overhears two peers discussing a case in a hospital café. They omit the patient's name but use a specific occupation, rare condition and small village. A visitor is seated nearby.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Quietly ask them to stop the discussion there and move it to a private appropriate place.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The combination of details can identify the patient even without their name.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Join the conversation and add the patient's age.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This increases the risk of identification in a public place.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether listeners could combine the details to recognise the person.
questions.explanation: Identifiability is the core confidentiality concern.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate action while the discussion is ongoing.
options: Raise the issue with the peers after they leave.
Pause the conversation and suggest a private room.
Ask aloud for more identifying details.
questions.explanation: Stop further disclosure discreetly; joining it makes the breach worse.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Remind the peers privately when the café conversation has finished.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: A private reminder helps future practice but allows a preventable disclosure to continue.

groups.title: Recording attendance
groups.stimulus: Student Gwen is leaving a placement early for a family matter. A classmate offers to mark her present for an afternoon tutorial, saying nobody would check. The course team has an absence-reporting process.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether there is a route to request authorised absence without sharing personal details widely.
questions.explanation: It affects how to notify appropriately, but not whether she can falsely claim attendance.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Let the classmate mark her present in exchange for doing the same later.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This recruits someone into falsifying records.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Decline the offer but wait until the next day to tell the course team despite being able to do so now.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: She avoids dishonesty; prompt communication would let the team plan appropriately.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the register is commonly audited.
questions.explanation: The chance of detection is irrelevant to honest reporting.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Explain that she cannot be marked present and use the absence-reporting process.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Honest reporting and a legitimate route address the situation without deception.

groups.title: Language support
groups.stimulus: A patient's adult son offers to interpret while a clinician explains an elective procedure. The patient turns away when possible complications are mentioned and has not been asked whether they want the son involved. A professional interpreter can be booked.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Assume the patient understands because the son says they both agree.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: A relative's reassurance does not establish the patient's understanding or agreement.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate proposal before consent is sought.
options: Ask the clinician to pause while translated written materials are located.
Arrange independent language support and confirm the patient's preference.
Accept the son's assent as the patient's consent.
questions.explanation: Appropriate support and choice are best; relying on family assent alone is worst.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Suggest to the clinician that the patient's language and interpreter preferences be checked privately with suitable support.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Accurate communication and a private choice support informed consent.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Provide generic written information in English as the only proposed fix.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Written information can help but does not resolve this language and consent concern.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the patient wants to discuss the procedure without the son present.
questions.explanation: The patient should be able to decide what is shared and with whom.

groups.title: An offer of coaching
groups.stimulus: A tutor offers student Imani extra coaching to help after a difficult placement. Near the end of the session he asks for a private social-media connection and repeatedly invites her to meet at his home rather than on campus. The tutor will assess her next week.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether coaching could continue with another tutor in an approved teaching setting.
questions.explanation: It offers a way to preserve learning support, but the immediate boundary concern still needs addressing.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Decline the invitation and contact a trusted course lead or reporting route for support.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The power imbalance and repeated private invitations make support and boundary-setting appropriate.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Ask another student for support but make no plan to contact an appropriate staff member.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Peer support is useful but cannot manage assessment conflict or a pattern of behaviour by itself.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the tutor has authority over Imani's upcoming assessment.
questions.explanation: The power imbalance is central to understanding the pressure.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Ask the tutor whether declining the private invitation will affect her assessment, and accept his verbal assurance without arranging independent support.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: It identifies the conflict, but leaves the concern within an unequal relationship rather than seeking a safe independent route.

groups.title: The wrong patient identifier
groups.stimulus: Under supervision, student Jay notices that a specimen label appears to use another patient's number. The specimen is about to be collected. Jay has never relabelled specimens and is unsure how the local process works.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Ask staff to stop collection while he immediately raises the discrepancy with his supervisor.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Preventing use of a potentially misidentified specimen is urgent; follow the local process.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Replace the label based on who he thinks provided the specimen.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Guesswork cannot reliably establish identity and may entrench the error.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate immediate response.
options: Write a replacement identifier from memory.
Ask the porter to wait briefly while looking for the local procedure.
Pause collection and tell the supervising clinician why.
questions.explanation: Halt the unsafe transfer and get supervision; guessing a label creates false certainty.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Ask the porter to return later without telling the clinical team why.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This can delay transport but leaves the safety problem unresolved.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the sample can be reliably linked to the person from whom it was taken.
questions.explanation: Safe processing requires clear identification.

groups.title: A difficult witness
groups.stimulus: During teaching, a registrar repeatedly makes dismissive remarks about a patient's accent after the patient leaves. Student Kiran sees another student laugh awkwardly. The placement has a confidential reporting system.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Tell the other student the remarks were unacceptable but leave the incident there.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Challenging the norm is helpful, but it may not address repeated conduct.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Post the registrar's name and the clinical encounter on a public forum.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Public disclosure risks harm and does not follow an appropriate process.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the behaviour could impair respectful care or discourage concerns from being raised.
questions.explanation: The context makes this a professionalism and safety issue rather than personal taste.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Raise a factual account through a safe supervisor or reporting route.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Disrespectful behaviour warrants a proportionate response, and reporting need not depend on peers agreeing.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether Kiran can distinguish what she heard directly from what she inferred.
questions.explanation: Accurate reporting matters; uncertainty about motive need not prevent reporting the remarks.

groups.title: The unconfirmed reference
groups.stimulus: Student Lena is helping prepare a teaching handout. A colleague has copied a numerical claim from a draft summary, but the original study actually reports a different result. The handout has not been distributed.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate way to handle the claim.
options: Publish the figure unchanged to meet the deadline.
Omit the unsupported item pending review.
Verify the figure and resolve the discrepancy before release.
questions.explanation: Check and amend with the colleague; knowingly retaining the false result is worst.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Keep the more striking figure because it makes the handout memorable.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Knowingly presenting an incorrect figure misleads learners.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Tell the colleague what differs and check the verified result together before distributing it.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This stops a known error and supports learning without blame.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether trainees may use the figure to guide future decisions.
questions.explanation: Potential downstream reliance increases the importance of accuracy.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Remove the claim without discussing why or checking related claims.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Removing misinformation helps, but the team misses a chance to correct the underlying source issue.

groups.title: A waiting patient
groups.stimulus: While shadowing in clinic, student Mina notices a patient who has been waiting a long time suddenly looking pale and saying they feel faint. The receptionist is on the phone and Mina does not know the patient's history.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? The sudden change in the patient's condition.
questions.explanation: New symptoms, not just waiting time, determine urgency.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Tell the patient to walk alone to another department to ask for help.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Walking alone when faint creates avoidable risk and delays assessment.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Offer reassurance but wait for the phone call to finish before telling anyone.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Reassurance can help, but unnecessary delay is unsafe when symptoms are new.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? How long the patient had been waiting before they began to feel faint.
questions.explanation: This may be useful background, but the new symptoms determine the need for assessment.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Alert available clinical staff immediately and stay nearby if safe, following their directions.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The change may need urgent assessment; Mina should summon someone competent promptly.

groups.title: A social invitation
groups.stimulus: A patient asks student Noah for his personal number so they can discuss test results after discharge. Noah knows the ward has a recognised contact number and that he does not have ongoing responsibility for the patient's care.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Explain the boundary and help the patient obtain the official number and follow-up information.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This protects boundaries while meeting a legitimate need for continuity.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Offer his number and promise to interpret later results independently.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: He cannot provide appropriate follow-up outside his role and approved channels.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the recognised route will allow a member of the care team to answer queries.
questions.explanation: A practical route protects continuity while maintaining boundaries.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Decline to share his number without explaining any route for follow-up.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Declining is right, but it leaves the patient's valid concern unmet.

groups.title: Restoring a wall
groups.stimulus: The village trust hired masons to repair an old boundary wall without moving its line. Some residents expected the repair to restore a perfectly straight top edge. A survey found that height varied in an early photograph, though sections rebuilt in the 1970s were almost level. The trustees concluded that making the whole wall level would reflect the later work rather than its earlier appearance. They retained some variations where they were structurally safe and replaced loose stones where needed. Several large stones looked ready to use, but a mason warned that hidden fractures could split them in cold weather. The team used them in low sections only after testing them. The trust chose to leave an opening that served as a route for hedgehogs, even though no surviving photograph showed that gap. It described the change on its website as an adaptation, not a reconstruction. A resident argued that a historical project should avoid anything undocumented. The trustees said that the wall needed to continue serving the village and that making a clearly identified adaptation was less misleading than letting people assume it was historic. Their final report listed repair materials and described the decision process but did not claim the photograph showed the original construction in every detail.

questions.stem: How did the trustees use the early photograph to make the repair decision?
options: They used the photograph to verify the shape of every stone.
They sought to reproduce exactly the repairs made in the 1970s.
They used visible height variation to justify keeping some uneven sections.
They inferred the height varied only because the wall's line had moved.
questions.explanation: The trustees regarded a uniformly level top as representative of later work, not the earlier appearance.

questions.stem: What does the treatment of the hedgehog opening illustrate?
options: The oldest photograph was treated as an exhaustive record.
All gaps were filled wherever photographs showed no opening.
The trust moved the wall to protect wildlife.
