An acknowledged adaptation can coexist with historical repair.
questions.explanation: The trust kept the opening for present use and identified it as an adaptation.

questions.stem: Which claim about the early photograph goes beyond the evidence?
options: It helped the trustees distinguish an earlier appearance from the 1970s repairs.
It influenced the choice to retain some existing variation.
It shows the wall before any repair had been made.
It shows that the top edge was not uniformly level.
questions.explanation: It documents one earlier appearance, not the wall's entire construction and repair history.

questions.stem: Why were some large stones restricted to low sections?
options: There was concern about hidden weaknesses in apparently suitable stones.
They were all imported in the 1970s.
The trustees needed to reserve them for the hedgehog gap.
There was a requirement to raise the whole wall.
questions.explanation: The mason warned of fractures; even after testing, reuse was limited.

groups.title: Matching volunteers
groups.stimulus: A coastal survey trained volunteers to record stranded objects on fixed stretches of shore. The first year's training gave everyone the same laminated pictures. New volunteers sometimes classified fragments as whole objects because the pictures showed only complete examples. In the next year trainers added images of broken items, but the number of reported fragments fell. A newspaper described this as evidence that the coast was cleaner. Trainers pointed out that the first year's survey included many beaches near a demolished pier, whereas access to those beaches was closed during the second year. They compared only beaches visited in both years and still found a smaller fall. However, teams had not visited each beach equally often, and the second year's surveys were clustered around calmer weather. One scientist suggested reporting count per visit and listing the weather differences rather than declaring a trend. The survey organisers adopted that suggestion. They also asked pairs of volunteers to classify the same finds independently on one stretch. The pairs agreed more often on intact items than fragments. The organisers used examples of disagreement in a refresher session. They did not remove the contested fragments from the published totals but listed the cases that could not be resolved in a separate category.

questions.stem: The set of beaches available in the second year differed from that in the first.
questions.explanation: The beaches near the demolished pier were surveyed in the first year but closed in the second.

questions.stem: The organisers excluded every contested fragment from the published results.
questions.explanation: Unresolved cases were retained as a separate category.

questions.stem: Training with broken-item images caused the fragment count to fall.
questions.explanation: The count fell after training changed, but locations, visits and weather also changed.

questions.stem: Paired classification showed that fractured objects drew less consistent judgements than intact ones.
questions.explanation: The pairs agreed more often on intact objects than on fragments.

groups.title: The lost footnote
groups.stimulus: A local history group scanned a booklet about the first public swimming baths in the district. Its online transcription described the baths as opening in May. In the printed original, a footnote distinguished the formal dedication in May from public admission in June. The scanner had captured the footnote, but the software arranged the text in reading order and placed the note after the index. The volunteer who proofread the main pages did not see it. A teacher spotted the problem when a pupil compared two sources for a project. The group fixed the date reference and added links from each note marker to its note. It also created a plain-text download for people whose reading software did not handle page links well. Some members asked whether the group should correct original spelling errors in that download. The editors chose to leave those spellings intact while appending explanations when they could seriously confuse a reader. The same policy did not apply to errors introduced by scanning, which the editors corrected wherever they found them. The group kept copies of page images available so that readers could distinguish the editors' intervention from the original printing. It did not claim that the original booklet was always accurate.

questions.stem: Who first identified the footnote issue, according to the account?
options: The volunteer proofreading the main pages
A teacher responding to a pupil's source comparison
A member arguing about original spelling
questions.explanation: The teacher noticed when the pupil compared two accounts.

questions.stem: What initially caused the footnote distinction to go unnoticed during proofreading?
options: The index listed a different public admission date from the note.
The volunteer relied on the plain-text download rather than the booklet.
The printed footnote was too faint for the scanner to capture.
The software placed the captured note outside the sequence the volunteer checked.
questions.explanation: It put the note after the index, beyond the main pages the volunteer proofread.

questions.stem: Why did the editors provide a plain-text download in addition to links within the transcription?
options: The note markers had no corresponding note after the correction.
Some readers' software might not handle the links well.
The plain-text file could reproduce the original page layout exactly.
The original booklet could not be captured as page images.
questions.explanation: The alternative made the content usable without depending on internal links.

questions.stem: Which distinction guided the editors' treatment of errors?
options: Date errors were always corrected in the page images.
Errors found by children were treated differently from those found by adults.
Original wording was preserved, whereas errors introduced by scanning were corrected.
Errors in the index were kept and all others corrected.
questions.explanation: The editors retained old spellings but fixed mistakes made by the process.

groups.title: Pond counts
groups.stimulus: A conservation team counted frogs at a restored pond on five evenings in its first spring. Volunteers looked and listened from a fixed station, taking care not to approach the water. In the second year more volunteers trained and counting took place on twelve evenings. The total number of recorded calls rose sharply. The project leader warned that a single frog can call repeatedly, so the total was not a head count. To make a more comparable measure she recalculated the mean number of calls per evening. That measure was higher too, but the second year's sessions were mostly warmer than those in the first. On two relatively cold evenings the count was low despite observations made the same way. The leader proposed recording temperature at each site and visiting an unrestored pond in the same season. A resident asked why the team did not count tadpoles instead. The leader said a tadpole survey would answer a related question about breeding, but results would depend on visibility and which parts of the pond were accessible. A funding statement described the restoration as promising, citing the range of wetland plants that had returned, while calling evidence of increasing frog numbers preliminary. The next survey plan retained call counts and added other indicators.

questions.stem: What makes the unrestored pond useful in the proposed survey?
options: It provides a comparison under some of the same seasonal conditions.
It allows all frogs to be counted directly at the restored pond.
It proves temperature has no influence on calling.
It ensures volunteer numbers cannot change.
questions.explanation: Same-season comparison can help separate wider conditions from restoration effects.

questions.stem: Why were total calls a poor measure of population growth?
options: The total fell while the nightly average rose.
Frogs were counted at the unrestored pond in year one instead.
The totals depended on surveying effort and repeated calls, not just frog numbers.
The observations only counted frogs visible on the banks.
questions.explanation: There were more observation evenings, and individual frogs could call repeatedly.

questions.stem: Why did dividing by the number of evenings not settle whether frog numbers rose?
options: The two samples still differed in temperature, which may affect calling.
The calculation treated visible tadpoles as adult frogs.
The second year's volunteers had stopped recording calls altogether.
The original survey took place at an unrestored pond.
questions.explanation: Standardising visits addresses survey effort but not the warmer observation conditions.

questions.stem: Which description best matches the funding statement?
options: Certain that restoration caused frog numbers to rise
Focused on breeding as the only valid measure
Encouraging about some outcomes but cautious about the frog population
Dismissive of both vegetation and frog observations
questions.explanation: It cites plant recovery and calls evidence on frogs preliminary.

groups.title: Complaints at the station
groups.stimulus: A train operator installed a single touch screen for passenger feedback at a busy station. It asked visitors to select a topic before typing comments. In the first month almost all complaints concerned cleanliness. Staff cleaned the toilets more often, but the next month's total complaints hardly changed. A passenger group noticed that 'toilets' appeared on the first screen, while lifts and announcements were only under 'other'. At that stage choosing 'other' also required typing a short description before the comment itself. The operator made all topics visible and removed that extra step. Complaints about lift access rose and comments about cleanliness occupied a smaller share of the total. Managers warned that the new mix did not establish whether lift access had become worse. They reviewed lift outage logs separately and recruited passengers who seldom used the screen for a short interview. Some interviewees said they had used another entrance and never passed the feedback point. The operator put a code on signs at both entrances linking to the same form but continued the interviews for those without smartphones. Its report showed figures before and after the redesign separately. It used them to identify issues to investigate, rather than as a single continuous indicator of station quality. It also logged the dates when the question order changed.

questions.stem: Why did the operator review lift outage logs separately?
options: The station had stopped carrying out interviews.
An increase in access complaints could reflect easier reporting rather than more outages.
There were no lift complaints before the redesign.
The feedback screen measured outage duration exactly.
questions.explanation: The interface change altered which topics were easy to select.

questions.stem: Which group were the interviews especially useful in reaching?
options: Staff who cleaned the toilets more than once a day.
Passengers who seldom used or did not pass the feedback screen.
Passengers who had already submitted a lift complaint on the screen.
Passengers who regularly used a smartphone to answer the form.
questions.explanation: Interviewees noted that some routes through the station never passed the feedback point.

questions.stem: What principle best explains reporting figures before and after separately?
options: An interview necessarily produces fewer complaints than a screen.
A change in measurement can change the observed pattern without a matching change in service.
Reports should exclude all feedback not given face to face.
Complaints can never help identify problems.
questions.explanation: The forms were not directly comparable as topic visibility and friction changed.

questions.stem: Which extra figure would determine whether fewer cleanliness comments were made after the redesign, given their shares and the previous total?
options: The total number of comments after the redesign.
The number of headings visible on the old screen.
The percentage of passengers who entered through the second entrance.
The number of lift outages after the redesign.
questions.explanation: The revised absolute count is the new share multiplied by the new total.

groups.title: Delivering the piano
groups.stimulus: An arts venue considered carrying a grand piano to its upper hall on an existing goods lift. The maintenance record listed a capacity well above the piano's weight. The engineer did not reject that figure but asked whether it assumed an evenly spread load. A drawing revealed that most of the piano's weight would rest on one end of its moving platform while it was rolled across the lift threshold. In addition, the hall doorway was wide enough on paper but a fire door closer reduced space at the angle needed to turn. The venue paid a specialist to model the turn and distribute the load. A donor offered to lend a smaller instrument, but the conductor said it would change the rehearsal plan. The venue retained the offer as a fallback and delayed advertising the concert until a dry run with an empty platform was complete. The dry run showed that existing floor protection would shift under the wheels. The specialist specified interlocking panels that would not move independently. In the published summary the venue described these as precautions identified by examining the route as a whole. It did not say the piano exceeded the lift's nominal capacity. For future events it asked organisers to provide dimensions and proposed movements along with weight.

questions.stem: What concern was not captured by the maintenance record's capacity figure?
options: When the donor offered an instrument
Whether the concert had been advertised
How the load was distributed as the piano crossed the threshold
Whether the conductor liked the rehearsal plan
questions.explanation: The engineer asked about even loading, then identified weight concentrated at one end.

questions.stem: What had the venue decided to do before advertising the concert?
options: Remove the fire door closer and remeasure the doorway.
Conduct a full rehearsal with the donor's piano.
Complete a dry run with an empty moving platform.
Check whether the piano was heavier than the lift's nominal limit.
questions.explanation: It delayed advertising until that dry run was complete.

questions.stem: What prompted the decision to specify interlocking panels?
options: The piano was heavier than the lift capacity.
The dry run showed the new panels were too narrow.
The empty platform showed the original protection would move under the wheels.
The door closer had been removed.
questions.explanation: Panels that did not move independently addressed the observed shift.

questions.stem: How did the venue treat the donor's offer?
options: It retained a possible backup without committing to change the instrument.
It adopted the smaller piano immediately once told the lift capacity.
It set aside its original route plan as soon as the offer was made.
It rejected the offer because the donor could not transport the instrument.
questions.explanation: The smaller piano was a fallback that would affect rehearsals if used.

groups.title: Free shelves
groups.stimulus: A community centre put a set of shelves near its entrance for visitors to exchange household items. When volunteers counted everything removed in a month, the exchange appeared busy. They were surprised that box lids and electrical cables accumulated while matching boxes and devices disappeared. A notice asked people to label items if more than one part was needed. In a second month volunteers counted fewer items, but recorded more complete sets finding new owners. A grant application used the latter measure to illustrate how the shelves could support reuse. It still listed separate small items, including cables, as useful to some visitors. A caretaker suggested taking away anything untouched for three days to prevent clutter. Volunteers preferred clearing the shelves on a published weekly schedule, because people using the centre on the same day each week might otherwise miss every item left just after their visit. They labelled separately a basket of things that were nearly due for removal. A charity agreed to take some leftovers but did not promise to accept every type of item. The centre kept a register of what it passed on and discarded. It did not claim to have measured exactly how much waste it prevented, because it did not know what donors and recipients would otherwise have done.

questions.stem: The grant application referred to complete sets finding new owners as evidence about reuse.
questions.explanation: It used the number of complete sets, a different outcome from the raw number of items taken.

questions.stem: The centre considered cables useless if left without an accompanying device.
questions.explanation: It regarded separate small items, including cables, as useful to some people.

questions.stem: The charity rejected at least one set of shelves.
questions.explanation: No rejection of shelving is described.

questions.stem: The weekly schedule was intended to improve the chance that weekly visitors would see items before clearance.
questions.explanation: That was the reason given for preferring weekly over three-day clearance.

groups.title: Copies of the key
groups.stimulus: Residents of a converted mill used a shared key to reach a roof garden. The managing committee introduced a numbered sign-out sheet after the key disappeared twice. At first, one volunteer kept the sheet and the key in an office next to the roof stairs. The key was almost never missing, but use by residents who worked late fell. One resident suggested cutting a key for every flat. The insurer permitted several authorised copies but required the committee to be able to identify who held each one. The committee instead introduced a lockbox for the shared key and issued individual codes. It retained a separate emergency key that could be used by the caretaker without entering a code. Records showed more visits after eight in the evening, though this overlapped with longer daylight hours. The minutes avoided crediting the lockbox with all of the increase. The committee nevertheless judged that residents could now obtain the key without relying on office opening hours. A survey pointed out a remaining problem: residents with restricted hand movement could find the lockbox stiff. At the following meeting the committee agreed to compare different boxes and ask several residents to test them before selecting a replacement. The garden remained open while this took place.

questions.stem: Which drawback of the staffed arrangement led to a practical change?
options: The sheet increased loss of the key.
Access depended on office opening hours.
The caretaker was prohibited from holding a spare.
The insurer prohibited numbered sign-out sheets.
questions.explanation: Late workers used the garden less when the key was held in the staffed office.

questions.stem: What constraint applied to the option of cutting several keys?
options: The committee needed to be able to identify the authorised holders.
The lockbox needed one common code to satisfy the insurer.
A caretaker could retain a key only by signing it out at the office.
Only the insurer could decide which residents would receive the original key.
questions.explanation: Several copies were permitted if each could be traced to a holder.

questions.stem: How did the committee plan to address the remaining access barrier?
options: Close the garden until the existing lockbox wore in.
Reinstate the staffed desk on all evenings.
Compare alternatives with help from residents who would use them.
Give the residents who reported difficulty a shared emergency code.
questions.explanation: It planned to test other boxes with residents before choosing a replacement.

questions.stem: Why did the minutes qualify the interpretation of evening visits?
options: Roof use might also have changed because evenings were lighter.
The garden had been closed throughout the comparison.
The visit sheet marked all visits incorrectly.
questions.explanation: The increase overlapped with longer daylight.

groups.title: Repairing a recording
groups.stimulus: An orchestra gave its archivist two recordings of the same concert, made from different locations in the hall. One had a persistent hum; the other lost a few seconds when a cable became loose. An engineer offered to patch the missing bars using the first recording. The archivist agreed for a listening copy but wanted an unaltered version retained for study. A producer suggested filtering out the hum wherever silence would otherwise make it noticeable. The engineer tested a filter and found that it also removed part of the low instruments' sound. Instead the team applied a more limited filter to the listening copy and left some noise. The liner notes described both the patch and the restricted filtering. A review praised the clarity of the final movement, which needed no patch but was among the sections where filtering was used. The orchestra made the listening version easy to stream and allowed researchers to request the two source recordings, subject to the performers' agreements. It did not stream the source recordings by default. The archivist argued that a reconstruction could be useful and honest if users were not led to mistake it for an untouched source. Later donations were logged with their original technical notes attached so that similar choices could be documented.

questions.stem: The team knowingly left some of the hum in order to preserve more of the instruments' sound.
questions.explanation: It limited filtering after finding that a more aggressive filter removed low instrument sound.

questions.stem: The final movement needed a patch from the first recording.
questions.explanation: It is described as needing no patch.

questions.stem: The complete recordings were made by the same engineer.
questions.explanation: The recordings' positions and technical faults are given, not who made them.

questions.stem: The archivist considered it misleading to offer a reconstructed copy even when its alterations were clearly described.
questions.explanation: The archivist considered a labelled reconstruction both useful and honest.

groups.title: Managing the crossing
groups.stimulus: A research group observed a road crossing used by staff leaving a trading estate. Its analysts used a camera to count people waiting, but the image was taken from one side and a shelter hid part of the queue. In week two an observer marked when the shelter was full and compared those notes with camera totals. The camera still registered some people as they stepped into view to cross. That made its crossing counts more useful than its estimates of how long people waited, because a person's arrival was often not seen. A councillor cited an apparently short camera-measured wait to argue against changing the signals. The analysts said the figures could not support that claim unaided. They later trialled a second camera from a position that showed the full queue without filming private windows. They also recorded the time the signal allowed pedestrians to cross. Simply extending the time pedestrians could be on the road might not reduce the interval before they were invited to start crossing. The report therefore recommended evaluating both durations separately. It distinguished waiting outside the crossing from crossing slowly with mobility aids. Staff continued observing at shift change because several workers said an average across the entire day would obscure the period when they needed the crossing most.

questions.stem: Why were camera counts of crossings more useful than camera estimates of waiting?
options: People often became visible when they began crossing, but not when they arrived.
The shelter was moved after the first week.
Signals were turned off every afternoon.
The camera recorded the time of every arrival reliably.
questions.explanation: The hidden queue obscured the start time needed for a wait estimate.

questions.stem: Which proposal could improve crossing conditions without necessarily reducing waiting time?
options: Moving the shelter to improve visibility to the first camera.
Allowing pedestrians more time to cross once invited to start.
Shortening the time between pedestrian phases while holding their length constant.
Comparing the queue with whole-day counts from other locations.
questions.explanation: That changes crossing duration, not necessarily the interval before the pedestrian phase.

questions.stem: What requirement shaped the second camera's position?
options: It had to show pedestrians after they left the trading estate but before they reached the queue.
It had to be installed at the same angle as the first camera.
It had to exclude people using the shelter entirely.
It had to show the full queue without recording private windows.
questions.explanation: The analysis needed arrivals without unnecessary filming of nearby property.

questions.stem: Why did the group continue observing at shift change?
options: The crossing operated only at shift change.
The shelter was shut the rest of the day.
A whole-day average might obscure conditions when workers most needed the crossing.
The team had ruled out comparing the two signal durations.
questions.explanation: Workers specifically identified the timing as important.

groups.title: A public clock
groups.stimulus: A town planned to repair its market hall clock, which had stopped during an unusually cold winter. The first appeal said the cold had broken the mechanism. When the repairer examined it, she found that dried oil increased friction even in warmer conditions. The cold might have made that problem worse, but she could not tell whether the clock would otherwise have stopped at a different time. An archive photograph showed a dial with Roman numerals; the present dial used Arabic numbers. The group considered switching back but found minutes from an earlier accessibility discussion recording complaints about reading the old dial from street level. Rather than choose between a readable clock and a historical display, it kept the current face and used the photograph in a sign under the tower. It corrected the appeal language to describe the cold as a possible contributor rather than a confirmed cause. Some supporters requested a demonstration of the repaired movement. Because the mechanism was above a narrow stair, the group arranged a live camera instead of opening the chamber. A survey of people who watched found interest in maintenance costs, so the group posted its annual service invoices. The invoice list did not show how long the clock had remained stopped in previous years.

questions.stem: How did the repairer's findings change the appeal's wording?
options: It treated cold as a possible contributing factor rather than a confirmed cause.
It said the failure would have occurred at exactly the same time in warm weather.
It credited dried oil as the sole cause in every past stoppage.
It made the change of numerals the explanation for the clock stopping.
questions.explanation: The dried oil was another factor and the role of cold was not established.

questions.stem: Why did the group retain the current dial?
options: It had evidence that the earlier dial could be hard to read from the street.
The current dial was identical to the historic one.
The older dial was known to be beyond repair.
questions.explanation: The minutes recorded visibility concerns, so the group showed the historic dial in a photo instead.

questions.stem: Why did the group offer a camera demonstration rather than open the chamber?
options: Supporters wanted invoices displayed next to the mechanism.
The camera was needed to obtain proof of the old numerals.
The mechanism could be seen without sending visitors up the narrow stair.
The clock had stopped again before people could enter.
questions.explanation: The physical access constraint prompted the use of a live feed.

questions.stem: What does the published invoice list directly help a reader check?
options: Whether dried oil caused each earlier failure
How long the clock was stopped each year
The date the old dial was replaced
How much the repair group paid for annual service
questions.explanation: The invoices relate to maintenance costs, not operational stoppage history.

questions.stem: Every workshop that uses a kiln requires ventilation. No basement workshop has ventilation. Some summer workshops use kilns. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some summer workshops are not in the basement.
All ventilated workshops use kilns.
No basement workshop uses a kiln.
No summer workshop is in the basement.
Some ventilated workshops are summer workshops.
questions.explanation: 1. The kiln-using summer workshops must have ventilation. 2. Ventilation may be provided for other reasons. 3. Using a kiln requires ventilation. 4. Other summer workshops may not use kilns. 5. The summer workshops with kilns are ventilated.

questions.stem: Five stalls A–E are numbered consecutively. E is in stall 3. D is immediately after B. C is after E. A is not adjacent to E. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: The valid orders are B–D–E–C–A. D is in position 2. This is the only option that holds in all of them.

questions.stem: A sleeve contains 17 samples of which 6 are labelled blue. Two are selected uniformly without replacement. What is the chance both are blue?
questions.explanation: 6/17 × 5/16 = 15/136. After a success, both the remaining successes and total fall by one.

questions.stem: Only A: 13; only B: 16; only C: 22; A and B only: 8; A and C only: 5; B and C only: 6; all three: 4; none: 18. How many attendees belong to exactly one of A and C, regardless of whether they belong to B?
questions.explanation: The relevant non-overlapping regions are A, C, AB, BC: 13 + 22 + 8 + 6 = 49.

questions.stem: A depot logs 210 dispatches on Monday and 140 on Tuesday, with 21 and 28 late respectively. On Wednesday it logs 50 dispatches with no late ones. What is the overall late rate, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: There are 49 late dispatches out of 400; 49/400 × 100 = 12.25%.

questions.stem: Every submission received by noon was checked. Only checked work was entered for a prize. Some bilingual submissions reached the office after noon. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some bilingual submissions were not checked.
Every prize entry was checked.
Some submissions arrived after noon.
Every checked submission was entered.
No unchecked submission arrived by noon.
questions.explanation: 1. Late submissions may still be checked. 2. Only checked submissions were entered. 3. The bilingual examples meet this condition. 4. Checking makes an entry possible, not mandatory. 5. Every submission arriving by noon was checked.

questions.stem: A show goes ahead if the venue and a technician are available. A technician is available only on Tuesday or Thursday. The venue is available on Monday and Thursday only. It is known that the show went ahead on one of the four days Monday–Thursday and requires both resources. On which day did it take place?
questions.explanation: Thursday is the only day in both availability sets.

questions.stem: A blind selection uses tray A with probability 2/3 and otherwise tray B. It then picks one tile uniformly from the selected tray. A has four arrow tiles out of 15; B has three arrow tiles out of 10. The tile picked has an arrow. What is the probability it came from A?
questions.explanation: The two success branches are 8/45 and 1/10. Of their combined probability, the first accounts for 8/45 ÷ (8/45 + 1/10) = 16/25.

questions.stem: Should a commuter service offer a quieter carriage with a no-calls rule? Select the strongest argument.
options: Yes; rules should be introduced whenever passengers disagree.
No; one extra sign would have to be printed.
No; passengers sometimes need to speak in public.
Yes; it would offer an option for passengers who need less noise without banning calls throughout the train.
questions.explanation: The proposal gives a targeted benefit while maintaining an alternative for callers.

questions.stem: Five files J–N are checked one at a time. N is checked third. M is immediately after J. L is before K. K is not next to N. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: The valid orders are J–M–N–L–K. M is in position 2. This is the only option that holds in all of them.

questions.stem: Total surveyed: 101. A: 37; B: 33; C: 31; A and B: 14; A and C: 11; B and C: 13; all three: 5. Pair counts include people in all three. How many people belong to A alone?
questions.explanation: Subtract the two overlaps in A, adding the triple back once because it was subtracted twice: 37 − 14 − 11 + 5 = 17.

questions.stem: Every object kept outdoors has a waterproof case. No object with a paper label has a waterproof case. Some old objects have paper labels. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: No paper-labelled object is kept outdoors.
Some old objects are not kept outdoors.
Every object with a waterproof case is stored outdoors.
No old object has a waterproof case.
Some old objects lack a waterproof case.
questions.explanation: 1. Outdoor storage requires a waterproof case. 2. The old paper-labelled objects cannot be outdoors. 3. It could be stored indoors too. 4. Other old objects may have cases. 5. Those with paper labels lack one.

questions.stem: A site records 90 journeys by bike, 150 on foot and 260 by car. Of bike journeys 40% are under 2 km; of foot journeys 80% are under 2 km; of car journeys 10% are under 2 km. Which mode accounts for the most journeys under 2 km?
questions.explanation: The estimated counts under 2 km are 36 by bike, 120 on foot and 26 by car.

questions.stem: Six of 20 seats are beside a window. Two different seats are allocated uniformly. What is the chance at least one is beside a window?
questions.explanation: Subtract the chance of two failures: 1 − 14/20 × 13/19 = 99/190.

questions.stem: Five gates F, G, H, I and Q open in order. G immediately follows Q. I opens first. H opens after F. H is not fifth. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: The valid orders are I–F–H–Q–G. H is in position 3. This is the only option that holds in all of them.

questions.stem: Should a town pause the sale of parking permits in streets where occupancy routinely exceeds capacity? Select the strongest argument.
options: No; some permit holders sometimes travel by train.
Yes; continuing to sell permits may give more residents access rights than the street can practically accommodate.
No; parking signs may have been printed recently.
questions.explanation: The answer directly addresses allocating scarce parking when demand regularly exceeds supply.

questions.stem: A grant cannot be renewed unless the previous report has been accepted. All projects in the extension programme had their grants renewed. Some youth projects are in the extension programme. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some youth projects had reports accepted.
Every accepted report led to renewal.
No extension project lacked an accepted report.
No non-youth project had its grant renewed.
Some youth projects had grants renewed.
questions.explanation: 1. Renewal for the extension projects required reports to be accepted. 2. Acceptance is only a prerequisite. 3. All extension projects had renewal. 4. The facts place no such limit. 5. Those in the programme did.

questions.stem: Total surveyed: 116. A: 43; B: 35; C: 36; A and B: 13; A and C: 14; B and C: 11; all three: 6. Pair counts include people in all three. How many do not belong to any of the groups?
questions.explanation: The union is 43 + 35 + 36 − 13 − 14 − 11 + 6 = 82; subtract from 116 to get 34.

questions.stem: Exactly one of the doors A, B and C is unlocked. A sign on A says 'B is unlocked'; on B it says 'C is locked'; on C it says 'A is locked'. Exactly one sign is true. Which door is unlocked?
options: The evidence does not determine it.
questions.explanation: If A is unlocked only B's sign is true; if C is unlocked only C's sign is true. Two solutions remain.

questions.stem: Five tasks A–E run in slots 1–5. A directly follows D. B is third. E is earlier than C. C is not next to B. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: The valid orders are D–A–B–E–C. E is in position 4. This is the only option that holds in all of them.

questions.stem: Nine of 25 files have colour illustrations. Two different files are selected uniformly. What is the probability exactly one has colour illustrations?
questions.explanation: Either order works: 2 × 9/25 × 16/24 = 12/25.

questions.stem: Should a large employer publish salary ranges on vacancies? Select the strongest argument.
options: No; other details of a job also matter.
Yes; it would make the text of each vacancy longer.
Yes; applicants can decide before applying whether the pay could meet their needs, reducing wasted effort for both sides.
No; some applicants find salaries difficult to compare.
questions.explanation: The argument identifies a practical benefit that directly follows from early access to pay ranges.

questions.stem: No borrowed instrument can be taken abroad without permit P. Every instrument carried on the tour was borrowed. At least one tour instrument was taken abroad. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: At least one instrument carried on the tour had permit P.
Every borrowed instrument had permit P.
Every instrument taken abroad without P was not borrowed.
All tour instruments were taken abroad.
There was a borrowed instrument taken abroad.
questions.explanation: 1. The borrowed tour instrument taken abroad required the permit. 2. Only overseas use creates the stated requirement. 3. A borrowed one could not be taken abroad without P. 4. At least one is not all. 5. At least one tour instrument meets both conditions.

questions.stem: Only A: 12; only B: 14; only C: 16; A and B only: 11; A and C only: 7; B and C only: 9; all three: 4; none: 17. How many respondents belong to B and at least one other group?
questions.explanation: The relevant non-overlapping regions are AB, BC, ABC: 11 + 9 + 4 = 24.

questions.stem: Of 160 workshops surveyed in winter, 48 had waiting lists. In summer, 54 of 180 did. The organiser says waiting-list prevalence rose. Which evaluation is best?
options: The number stayed the same and the proportion fell.
The summer prevalence rose by six percentage points.
The counts rose but the proportions were the same.
Both the number and the proportion fell.
questions.explanation: 48/160 and 54/180 are both 30%; six is the difference in counts, not percentages.

questions.stem: Five pitches P–T start in order. S is immediately after Q. R is second. P is before T. T is not in fifth position. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: The valid orders are P–R–T–Q–S. S is in position 5. This is the only option that holds in all of them.

questions.stem: Five of 21 identical tickets conceal a prize. Two are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability both conceal a prize?
questions.explanation: 5/21 × 4/20 = 1/21. After a success, both the remaining successes and total fall by one.

questions.stem: If a plot receives irrigation, it is inspected. No inspected plot is completely inaccessible. Some leased plots are completely inaccessible. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some leased plots are not irrigated.
Every inspected plot receives irrigation.
No irrigated plot is completely inaccessible.
Some leased plots are not inspected.
No leased plot receives irrigation.
questions.explanation: 1. Inaccessibility rules out inspection and hence irrigation. 2. The first implication cannot be reversed. 3. Irrigation implies inspection, which excludes total inaccessibility. 4. The inaccessible leased plots cannot be inspected. 5. Other leased plots may be accessible and irrigated.

questions.stem: A panel chooses one person from each pair: A/B, C/D and E/F. Choosing A forces D; choosing E rules out D. Which trio could be selected?
questions.explanation: B/C/E meets all three pair requirements and does not combine E with D. The other trios break one stated implication.

questions.stem: Should large parks retain some unmown areas through the summer? Select the strongest argument.
options: Yes; uncut grass is always more attractive.
No; a park can never serve two purposes.
No; some visitors arrive by bus.
Yes; selected unmown areas can provide habitat while other areas remain available for recreation.
questions.explanation: The argument explains a relevant ecological benefit and recognises the continuing recreational use.

questions.stem: All members of team X submitted a portfolio. No submission after the deadline received feedback. Some members of X received feedback. Assume all feedback referred to a submitted portfolio. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some portfolios submitted by X were not late.
Every portfolio submitted on time received feedback.
No late portfolio received feedback.
Some members of X were not given feedback.
All feedback recipients belonged to X.
questions.explanation: 1. The feedback recipients could not have submitted late. 2. On-time submission does not guarantee feedback. 3. This is stated explicitly. 4. All could have received feedback. 5. Feedback to other submitters is not excluded.

questions.stem: In a class, 18 students do a practice task and 15 pass. The 12 who do not practise include 6 who pass. Which claim is best supported?
options: The difference in pass rates is exactly 9 percentage points.
The group that practised had a higher observed pass rate.
More than half of non-practising students passed.
questions.explanation: 15/18 is about 83%; 6/12 is 50%. The comparison alone does not establish cause.

questions.stem: Only A: 16; only B: 14; only C: 11; A and B only: 7; A and C only: 5; B and C only: 6; all three: 3; none: 12. How many people belong to A or B but not to both, including people also in C?
questions.explanation: The relevant non-overlapping regions are A, B, AC, BC: 16 + 14 + 5 + 6 = 41.

questions.stem: All three switches A, B and C are either on or off. If A is on, B is off. If B is off, C is on. Exactly one switch is on. Which assignment is possible?
options: None of the switches is on.
Only A is on, and this is the only possible assignment.
questions.explanation: With only C on both rules hold. A alone would require C as well; A and C or none violate the exact-one rule.

questions.stem: Five of 12 routes are steep. A system picks one route uniformly each day and choices are independent. What is the chance that both of the next two routes are steep?
questions.explanation: Replacement keeps each probability at 5/12; multiply the two chances to get 25/144.

groups.title: Greenhouse trial
groups.stimulus: Masses are in kilograms. Each bed covers the area shown. Marketable crop is a percentage of total harvested mass.

questions.stem: What is the combined marketable mass from East and West?
questions.explanation: ((69 × 80) + (95 × 70)) ÷ 100 gives 121.7 kg to the stated precision.

questions.stem: How much greater is South's marketable yield per square metre than West's, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: (((80 × 85) ÷ 20) − ((95 × 70) ÷ 24)) ÷ 100 gives 0.63 kg/m² to the stated precision.

questions.stem: If total harvest at North rises 20% but the marketable share drops 7 percentage points, find the new marketable mass.
questions.explanation: ((54 × 1.2) × (92 − 7)) ÷ 100 gives 55.08 kg to the stated precision.

questions.stem: What percentage of the total harvest of all beds was non-marketable? Give one decimal place.

groups.title: Ferry fares
groups.stimulus: Bike surcharge is per person and does not receive other discounts. Return fares below are per person and cover both directions.

questions.stem: What does a Cedar return cost for 4 adults and 3 children, with 5 bikes?
questions.explanation: ((23 × 4) + (14 × 3)) + (6 × 5) gives £164.00 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: Dale applies 15% off all return fares. How much is paid by three adults and one child taking a bike each?
questions.explanation: (((28 × 3) + 17) × 0.85) + (7.5 × 4) gives £115.85 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: You buy 2 adult and 2 child returns on each of Alder and Birch, with no bikes. What percentage of the combined cost is spent on Birch? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: ((18 + 12) ÷ (((14 + 8) + 18) + 12)) × 100 gives 57.7% to the stated precision.

questions.stem: A child with a bike switches from Cedar to Dale with two adults without bikes. What is the increase in the total cost?

groups.title: Print room
groups.stimulus: The fixed charge is applied once per print job. The ink price is charged per sheet even if the sheet is printed on both sides; use the stated sheets per copy.

questions.stem: How much are 450 programmes as one job?
questions.explanation: 20 + ((8 × (0.05 + 0.025)) × 450) gives £290.00 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: How much less do 175 posters cost than 175 guides, each as a separate job?
Ink for flyers goes up by 25%. What is the revised cost per copy if 400 copies are ordered, including the fixed charge, to three decimal places?
How much is saved by combining 5 identical orders of 120 programmes into one job, if the printer also offers 10% off the ink for the combined volume?

groups.title: Orienteering routes
groups.stimulus: Distances are one way. Each group walks the route at its constant stated pace except for the separate checkpoint stop; assume an uninterrupted return at the same pace if requested.

questions.stem: How many minutes does it take to reach the end of Red, including its stop?
How many minutes longer is the outward journey on Gold than on Blue, each with its stop?
For an out-and-back on Green with only one stop overall, what is the average speed to two decimal places including the stop?
questions.explanation: (4.5 × 2) ÷ (((4.5 × 2) ÷ 3.6) + (6 ÷ 60)) gives 3.46 km/h to the stated precision.

questions.stem: A Blue walker has 60 minutes to reach the endpoint including their stop. At what constant walking speed must they travel?
questions.explanation: 5.4 ÷ ((60 − 12) ÷ 60) gives 6.75 km/h to the stated precision.

groups.title: Community savings
groups.stimulus: Interest is paid annually and compounded. There are no withdrawals, charges or deposits after the opening deposit.

questions.stem: How much interest does Craft earn by maturity?
questions.explanation: ((1400 × 1.04) × 1.04) − 1400 gives £114.24 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: What is Youth's maturity balance to the nearest pound?
How much more interest does Sport earn than Garden in their first two years?
What extra deposit would Sport need at opening to mature at £2,205 at its original rate?
questions.explanation: ((2205 ÷ 1.05) ÷ 1.05) − 1600 gives £400.00 to the stated precision.

groups.title: Paving inventory
groups.stimulus: Packs may not be split for purchase. Use exact areas; no cutting loss unless specified. All tiles are square.

questions.stem: How much does it cost to buy enough Slate for 10.4 m²?
questions.explanation: (round up to a whole number of (10.4 ÷ (((25 ÷ 100) × (25 ÷ 100)) × 12))) × 18 gives £252.

questions.stem: What area can 15 packs of Chalk cover?
questions.explanation: (((20 ÷ 100) × (20 ÷ 100)) × 18) × 15 gives 10.8 m² to the stated precision.

questions.stem: A 4 m by 3 m terrace uses Sand. Allow an extra 10% of area for waste. What is the minimum purchase price?
How many more Slate than Moss packs are needed to cover 9 m²?
questions.explanation: (round up to a whole number of (9 ÷ (((25 ÷ 100) × (25 ÷ 100)) × 12))) − (round up to a whole number of (9 ÷ (((50 ÷ 100) × (50 ÷ 100)) × 6))) gives 6 packs.

groups.title: Rainwater trial
groups.stimulus: Matched gauges serve four collections. One millimetre of rain on one square metre supplies one litre before collection losses.

questions.stem: How many litres did the Studio and Garage collect in total, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: (((45 × 31) × 80) + ((32 × 28) × 85)) ÷ 100 gives 1877.6 L to the stated precision.

questions.stem: How many litres would the Cafe collect if its catchment grew by 10 m² and its collected share rose by 8 percentage points?
What was the combined collected share for the Cafe and Shop, weighted by available litres, to two decimal places?
How many more litres ran off without collection at the Cafe than at the Garage, to one decimal place?

groups.title: Training completion
groups.stimulus: Completers are counted once per cohort. The course fee is per enrollee; the bursary share is a percentage of the course fee for every enrollee in that cohort.

questions.stem: What is the combined completion rate in autumn, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: ((57 + 69) ÷ (75 + 92)) × 100 gives 75.4% to the stated precision.

questions.stem: What is the total bursary spend for Spring A?
questions.explanation: ((84 × 130) × 30) ÷ 100 gives £3276.00 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: How much more fee income after bursaries was collected from Autumn B than Spring B?
How many additional original Spring A enrollees would need to complete to bring that cohort's completion rate to at least 90%?
questions.explanation: (round up to a whole number of (84 × 0.9)) − 63 gives 13 people.

groups.title: Gallery footfall
groups.stimulus: Tuesday to Friday figures are independent daily counts. Each paying adult pays the listed price; children's tickets are half price. Free admissions are counted separately.

questions.stem: What is Friday's total ticket revenue?
questions.explanation: (79 + (42 ÷ 2)) × 8.5 gives £850.00 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: What percentage of the total admissions on Tuesday and Wednesday combined were free? Give one decimal place.
Thursday's adult price is reduced by £1, and 10 extra paying adults visit. At the new price structure, what is Thursday's new revenue? The child fee remains half the adult price.
questions.explanation: ((52 + 10) + (33 ÷ 2)) × (8 − 1) gives £549.50 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: What is the overall mean ticket revenue per admission on Tuesday, including free admissions? Give the nearest penny.
questions.explanation: ((58 + (24 ÷ 2)) × 7) ÷ ((58 + 24) + 15) gives £5.05 to the stated precision.

groups.title: Before the briefing
groups.stimulus: Student Orla receives an updated care-team briefing that she realises is intended for another student not on her current placement. The document contains patient details; the email has also gone to multiple other recipients.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether all recipients were authorised and whether further forwarding is possible.
questions.explanation: Scope and ongoing exposure matter to containment.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Report the mistaken disclosure promptly via the placement's approved route and follow containment instructions.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The breach can then be assessed and other recipients contacted appropriately.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Delete the email locally without letting anyone know.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Local deletion may reduce access but does not address the multiple misdirected copies.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate response.
options: Tell the sender privately to check the recipients.
Notify the approved team without unnecessary patient detail.
Forward the attachment to the course group to demonstrate the error.
questions.explanation: Use the incident pathway; redistributing sensitive detail worsens the breach.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Reply all with patient details to demonstrate that the file was sent incorrectly.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This repeats the disclosure to the wrong audience.

groups.title: Too many tasks
groups.stimulus: An exhausted student, Priya, is asked to prepare notes for a round and escort a patient to an appointment at the same time. She finds it hard to concentrate and has just confused two room numbers. Another team member is available.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Complete the notes first and explain the escort delay afterward.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Choosing unilaterally could delay needed care; flag the conflict first.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether Priya can describe her recent mix-up without revealing unnecessary patient details.
questions.explanation: Clear, discreet disclosure helps the team understand the issue while protecting privacy.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Accept both tasks and rely on memory despite the recent confusion.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Concealing fatigue and overload risks another error.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether either task is time-critical for the patient.
questions.explanation: Clinical urgency should inform safe prioritisation.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Tell the supervising team she cannot safely do both and agree what to hand over.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The team can reprioritise with knowledge of a real safety concern.

groups.title: An uncertain entry
groups.stimulus: Student Reece writes the wrong time for a discussion in a patient record. The team has not used the entry yet. The system permits dated amendments preserving earlier versions.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Make a transparent correction using the approved amendment process and alert the team if the error could affect care.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This restores accuracy while keeping the audit trail.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the recorded time affects a current clinical decision.
questions.explanation: This determines how urgently people need to be told.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Ask another student to edit it under their account so Reece's error is less visible.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This hides accountability and falsely attributes the amendment.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate response.
options: Tell one team member while awaiting advice on making an amendment.
Ask a peer to make an untraceable correction for Reece.
Correct the time through the formal amendment process.
questions.explanation: An auditable correction is best; disguising responsibility is worst.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Tell the next team orally but leave the electronic entry unchanged.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The warning helps those present but other readers could still rely on the error.

groups.title: The quiet colleague
groups.stimulus: Student Saira sees a colleague being interrupted repeatedly when trying to raise a concern about a patient in a team meeting. The chair says there is no more time. Saira knows the issue may affect a decision being taken that afternoon.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Assume silence means the colleague's concern was resolved.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Being interrupted is not evidence that the risk was assessed.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Tell the colleague she agrees it should have been heard, but wait until tomorrow to raise it.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Support helps, but a time-sensitive issue may already affect patient care.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Support the colleague to get the concern heard promptly by the responsible clinician.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Ensure the decision maker hears a potentially important safety concern in time.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the meeting minutes will include a note about the interruption.
questions.explanation: It could help later review, but does little to get the concern heard before the decision.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the clinical decision is imminent.
questions.explanation: It determines the need for escalation before the meeting's decision is acted on.

groups.title: Refusing observation
groups.stimulus: An outpatient says they do not want students to observe a consultation about a sensitive problem. Student Tariq has travelled a long distance to the clinic. The doctor asks if he can remain for just the first part.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Remain quietly because the doctor has invited him to stay.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: A staff invitation does not override the patient's refusal.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether declining observation changes the patient's access to care.
questions.explanation: The patient must be able to decline without a penalty.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate response to the refusal.
options: Leave now and ask staff later about other teaching opportunities.
Stay at the back despite the refusal.
Leave and ask the doctor privately to clarify the student introduction process.
questions.explanation: Leave respectfully; missing a learning opportunity does not justify ignoring refusal.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Leave only after describing the effort involved in travelling to the clinic.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Leaving is right, but invoking inconvenience can pressure the patient.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Respect the patient's refusal and leave, discussing alternative learning privately later.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Patient choice takes priority over the inconvenience to a student.

groups.title: An unfamiliar skill
groups.stimulus: Student Una is asked to use a device she has only seen once. The qualified operator is called away before the patient arrives. There is time to ask the placement lead for help.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether a qualified alternative operator is available nearby.
questions.explanation: This affects how to arrange care with minimal delay, but does not permit Una to proceed unsupervised.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Explain her limits and arrange qualified supervision before using the device.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: A patient should not be exposed to unsupervised practice beyond her competence.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Proceed because the operator originally expected to be there.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: An initial plan for oversight is not the same as supervision now.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Read the guide and prepare the room while waiting for a qualified person.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Useful preparation, provided it does not substitute for obtaining supervision.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether delay could harm the patient and require prompt reassignment.
questions.explanation: The team can arrange safe, timely care if it knows the urgency.

groups.title: A public fundraising post
groups.stimulus: A friend asks student Vik to share a fundraising post for someone on his ward. The fundraiser is public, but the person has not told Vik he may disclose anything he knows from placement. The friend asks whether a detail in the post is accurate.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Avoid confirming placement information and keep any reply to general, public facts.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Public claims do not permit disclosure of what was learned in a clinical role.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the information Vik would independently confirm came from his placement.
questions.explanation: The source and nature of the information determine confidentiality obligations.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Decline without discussing details, but tell the friend that an unnamed hospital employee could verify it.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: He avoids direct disclosure but invites unauthorised confirmation elsewhere.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate reply.
options: Send a screenshot of the medical record to confirm it.
Say he cannot confirm private information learned on placement.
Avoid answering the diagnosis question and point to the public post only.
questions.explanation: A clear boundary protects confidentiality; copying the private record creates a direct breach.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Confirm the diagnosis from the record because the fundraiser mentions it already.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Verifying a private fact using clinical access is a further disclosure.

groups.title: The mixed-up schedule
groups.stimulus: Student Willa notices an appointment reminder about a patient has gone to an incorrect mobile number. Her colleague suggests silently correcting the number and moving on. The intended patient is at risk of missing the appointment.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Fix the number for future messages but do not check this appointment.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: It limits recurrence but neglects current continuity and the breach.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Text the incorrect number with more patient details to ask it to delete the previous message.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: That adds an unauthorised disclosure; follow the incident team's advice instead.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Use the incident route, correct the contact details through approved steps and ensure the team can reach the intended patient.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Both the disclosure and continuity of care need a response.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the message includes information that could identify the patient.
questions.explanation: That affects the nature and seriousness of the incident.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the last system upgrade made this error easier to make.
questions.explanation: That is useful for preventing recurrence but secondary to containing this incident and reaching the patient.

groups.title: A strained conversation
groups.stimulus: A relative is upset that a discharge date changed. Student Xavier witnessed a private team discussion but is not authorised to make or explain the decision. The patient has not said what may be shared with the relative.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Acknowledge the frustration and arrange for the responsible clinician to speak with the patient and appropriately with the relative.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Responds empathetically while respecting confidentiality and scope.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Repeat the whole private discussion to calm the relative.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Distress does not authorise disclosure.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Give the relative the correct ward number but make no attempt to help them find an appropriate member of the team now.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The number is useful but a direct handover would better address the immediate concern.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate response.
options: Offer to contact the appropriate clinician without discussing private details.
Reveal the private discussion without checking the patient's wishes.
Provide the ward contact information without disclosing details.
questions.explanation: Validate the concern and route it correctly; using private details to appease the relative breaches trust.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the patient has given permission to share the specific information.
questions.explanation: The patient's preferences determine what can be disclosed in this situation.

groups.title: An incorrect dose list
groups.stimulus: Student Yara notices that a printed transfer sheet has a different medicine dose from the electronic plan. The receiving team is preparing to act on the sheet, and Yara does not know which dose is current.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Leave a message for someone to check it at the end of the shift.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The message may arrive after the sheet has been acted on.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the receiving team might use the disputed dose before the difference is resolved.
questions.explanation: Potential imminent use makes escalation urgent.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Choose whichever dose looks more familiar and tell the team to use it.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Familiarity is not verification and could cause harm.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the printed sheet uses the newest visual layout.
questions.explanation: Layout does not establish the correct dose.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Flag the discrepancy immediately and ask the responsible clinician to reconcile it before use.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Escalate promptly without guessing which source is correct.

groups.title: Accommodating a colleague
groups.stimulus: Student Zahra's teammate explains that they cannot read text on a low-contrast slide deck. Zahra is responsible for uploading the materials and can make an accessible copy without changing its clinical content.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Announce the teammate's presumed diagnosis to explain the format change.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: That discloses or invents private information without need.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Ask what format works, make an accessible version and check it is available for the session.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Practical adjustment based on the person's preference supports participation.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the revised material can be shared without exposing the teammate's private information.
questions.explanation: It affects implementation; private details are not needed to make the adjustment.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Send the teammate a larger copy without checking whether it resolves the contrast problem.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: It is a useful attempt but may not meet the stated access need.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate response.
options: Offer a provisional high-contrast copy pending feedback.
Ask the teammate privately about a suitable accessible version.
Tell the whole group the teammate's presumed medical reason.
questions.explanation: Make a useful adjustment without singling the person out; public speculation breaches trust.

groups.title: A sporting gift
groups.stimulus: At the end of a placement, a patient offers student Abe expensive match tickets. The patient has another appointment the following week and jokes that the gift might get them seen faster. The placement has a gifts policy.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Accept privately and assure the patient he will move the appointment forward.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This links a valuable gift to improper preference.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether accepting could be seen as influencing access to care.
questions.explanation: The comment about priority makes the conflict of interest direct.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Thank the patient, decline the tickets and seek advice under the gifts policy.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This maintains boundaries and avoids the appearance of preferential treatment.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the team Abe supports is playing in the match.
questions.explanation: His personal interest does not determine professional boundaries.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Refuse without explanation and immediately leave the conversation.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: It avoids accepting the gift, but a courteous explanation would protect trust.

groups.title: A private chat screenshot
groups.stimulus: A study group uses fictional cases in a chat. Student Bev notices a new screenshot from an actual record with names and a date of birth. Another member suggests that everyone delete it and keep quiet.

questions.stem: Select the most and least appropriate response.
options: Ask the sender to remove the original chat message.
Send it to another social group as a warning.
Stop onward sharing and seek official incident advice.
questions.explanation: Contain and report; sharing copies creates further harm.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Ask members not to forward the image and notify the authorised placement route promptly.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Stop further spread and let the responsible team manage containment.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Delete the screenshot personally without telling anyone else.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This reduces Bev's own access but leaves the wider disclosure unresolved.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Download additional copies to show friends what happened.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: That extends exposure unnecessarily.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether group members received or forwarded identifiable information.
questions.explanation: The scope of disclosure informs the response.

groups.title: The delayed introduction
groups.stimulus: Student Chen is allowed to take a supervised history. The patient thinks Chen is a qualified doctor and asks whether they can stop a treatment immediately. The supervisor is in the next room.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Pretend to be qualified and tell the patient to stop the treatment.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This is both deceptive and unsafe.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Explain his role and tell the patient that he cannot answer, without offering to get the supervisor.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Honest limits are appropriate but active handover would better support the patient.

questions.stem: How appropriate is the following response? Clarify his student role and arrange prompt review by the supervising clinician rather than advising a change himself.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The patient deserves accurate role information and advice from someone competent.

questions.stem: How important is the following consideration? Whether the request concerns an immediate change in care.
questions.explanation: The urgency affects how promptly Chen should get qualified help.
